# DevSecOps Challenge 1 — DevSecOps with Coding Agents at Papaya

## Note

- You are required to use a coding agent (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor) to complete this challenge.
- If you have any issues or questions, don't hesitate to contact us.

## Context

Papaya builds a GenAI-powered enterprise platform for the insurance industry — Claim, Underwriting, Policy Servicing, and FWA (Fraud/Waste/Abuse) — serving insurer partners across SEA and Asia. Our platform processes sensitive data every day: medical documents, diagnoses, claim histories, national IDs, and bank accounts of insured members.

Every engineer at Papaya works agent-first: Claude Code (Team Premium) is the primary tool for writing code, running git, opening PRs, and increasingly for infrastructure work.

This is where we are today (see [Appendix A](#appendix-a--papaya-platform-context) for the full picture):

- Engineers run Claude Code on their laptops, signed in to AWS through their SSO profiles. Most engineers' profiles can reach production.
- Some engineers run Claude Code with permission prompts turned off because "it is faster".
- Engineers install MCP servers and plugins they find useful; there is no review process.
- CI/CD runs on GitHub Actions. Some workflows use a long-lived GitHub token and AWS access keys stored as repository secrets.
- Monitoring and alerting exist but are fragmented across CloudWatch, GCP, and Slack channels. On-call is informal.
- We are working towards ISO 27001 and must satisfy HIPAA and regional data-protection regulations for our partners.

We've heard two strong opinions from inside the company:

> **Engineering:** "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly. I want to debug and ship my own infra changes without waiting for someone else."
>
> **Compliance:** "Nothing changes in production — by a human or an agent — without a named person who reviewed and approved it."

## Problem

You are joining as our DevSecOps Engineer. Your first mission: **design the framework and workflow for how Papaya uses coding agents for DevSecOps.**

You don't have access to our systems or code, and we don't expect you to.

## Requirements

- The format of the deliverable is up to you.

## Submission

Submit everything in **one GitHub repository** and send us the link. Other channels (cloud storage, email attachments) are not accepted.

The repository must contain:

- Your deliverable(s).
- The **complete, raw, unedited conversation(s)** with your coding agent — every session you used for this challenge. Native session files are preferred (e.g. Claude Code: `~/.claude/projects/**/*.jsonl`; Codex CLI: `~/.codex/sessions/`); for chat apps, commit an export of the conversation.

**Submissions without the agent conversation will be automatically marked as failed.**

---

## Appendix A — Papaya Platform Context

### Cloud

- **AWS (primary):** Lambda (Serverless Framework), ECS, EC2, Aurora PostgreSQL, SNS, SQS, Step Functions, S3 (claim documents), CloudWatch.
- **GCP:** Vertex AI and Gemini API workloads for document AI and ML models.
- **Kubernetes ([k0s](https://k0sproject.io/)):** workloads for AI agents and internal services.
- **Hosting:** Firebase Hosting for web frontends.

### Application

- **Backend:** Node.js, TypeScript, GraphQL (Apollo Server, Hasura), PostgreSQL.
- **Frontend / Mobile:** Next.js, React, React Native (Expo).
- **AI/ML:** Python, PyTorch, OpenAI, Vertex AI, Gemini, Claude.
- **AI agents in production:** claim assessment, document extraction and classification, FWA detection — they read documents uploaded by partners and members.

### Engineering

- **Source control & CI/CD:** a single monorepo on GitHub for the whole system — apps, web, backend, mobile, AI/ML, and Infrastructure as Code ([Pulumi](https://www.pulumi.com/), plus [Serverless Framework](https://www.serverless.com/) for Lambda functions); GitHub Actions for CI/CD.
- **Coding agent:** Claude Code (Team Premium) for every engineer; internal Claude Code plugins are distributed via a plugin marketplace.
- **Work tracking & communication:** Linear, Slack.
- **Tenancy:** multiple insurer partners across countries (e.g. Vietnam, Thailand, Hong Kong), each with their own data and contractual requirements.

### Compliance

- ISO 27001 (in progress), HIPAA, and regional data-protection regulations in the countries we operate in.
========
# Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1 — Coding Agents for DevSecOps

Submission for [DevSecOps Challenge 1](https://github.com/papaya-insurtech/pumpkin/blob/main/Hiring/DevSecOps_Challenges/DevSecOps_Challenge_1.md)
(local copy: [work/00-challenge.md](work/00-challenge.md)).

> Status: complete; all documents approved by the owner · Updated: 2026-11-09

## The problem and the answer

Engineering wants Claude Code to talk to AWS directly; Compliance wants nothing to change in
production without a named human who reviewed and approved it. The two only disagree about **writes
to production**: reads of metadata and all of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence.

The answer ("A + D2'", owner decision): **every prod change is a pull request**, approved by a code
owner who is not the author and applied by CI, incidents included. A time-boxed, approved JIT grant,
used by a human without an agent, is the only fallback during an incident when the PR path cannot be
used. Nobody, human or agent, holds standing prod write or long-lived credentials (one exception:
k0s/Firebase CI deploy credentials, kept as `production` environment secrets, OD1).

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free non-prod loop with the agent; read-only prod metadata | Approval **before** apply by a named human ≠ author, enforced by GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent |
| One approval, same-day ship; incident approval ≤ 15 min, 24/7 | One evidence chain per change; target ≤ 30 min to retrieve it, realistic from phase 2 |
| **Costs:** slower incident lane (est. 11–46 min); no raw logs of unredacted services at first; more prompts; 24/7 approver duty; ≤ 5 days for a new tool | **It does not give:** a technical stop on an agent approving through its engineer's login; prevention of admins editing the gate (logged only) |

**Where it falls short** (stated in [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page)):
the JIT fallback meets the approval rule only partly; on GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before
apply, so a risk stop holds risky diffs for a second approval; high-risk (L3) changes get one
approver, from the owners of the path; admins can edit the gate (logged, not prevented); on normal
days domain review by the on-call group is a process rule; "an agent never approves a PR" is
policy and training, not a technical control; k0s and Firebase are weaker; if the required-check GitHub App is down, every merge is blocked, incident PRs included; whether HIPAA applies is a
legal question.

## How to read it

| You are | Read | Time |
|---|---|---|
| Decision panel | This page, [framework §1](docs/01-framework.md#1-the-decision-in-one-page), [rollout plan](docs/03-rollout-plan.md), [diagrams](diagrams/README.md) | ~15 min |
| Compliance | [Compliance register](docs/04-compliance-mapping.md), [threat model](docs/05-threat-model.md), [problem → control map](docs/06-problem-control-map.md) | ~45 min |
| Engineer | [Engineer guide](docs/02-engineer-guide.md), [examples](examples/README.md), framework layers 1–3 | ~45 min |

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| [docs/](docs/) | Framework (8 layers: principle, Papaya's stack, audit evidence, cost/value), guide, rollout, register, threat model, map, [ADRs](docs/adr/README.md) |
| [examples/](examples/README.md) | Ruleset, CODEOWNERS, workflows, a runnable risk stop, IAM/OIDC/SCP, managed settings, plugin marketplace, policy pack; each with a local check and what it does **not** prove |
| [diagrams/](diagrams/README.md) | Change workflow, trust boundaries, incident lane |
| [work/](work/) | Working notes and decision log (Vietnamese, with English summaries) |
| [transcripts/](transcripts/) | Complete, raw, unedited Claude Code session files |
| [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) | The rules the agent followed in this repository |

## Evidence markers

Every claim about a tool carries one: ✅ verified here · 📖 official documentation, with a link or a research row `R x.y` in
[work/02-research.md](work/02-research.md) · ⚠️ inference or not verified · [design] my proposal, untested.
Nothing was run against Papaya's systems; I had no access to them.

## How this was built

The repository was written with Claude Code under the same approach it recommends:

- [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) set the rules: source markers, no secrets, design only.
- From the research step on, each step went to an **independent reviewer subagent** (given the file
  and the criteria, not my conclusions) until no HIGH/MEDIUM finding remained or the owner stopped the
  rounds; [the log](work/session-log.md) notes fixes that were not re-reviewed. The framing was reviewed with the owner.
- **Deviation:** `CLAUDE.md` planned Manual permission mode from session 2, but the VS Code extension
  started most working sessions in **auto mode** (transcripts record `permissionMode: "auto"`;
  `"default"` only in three short sessions, ✅ grep). Auto mode is allowed by choice (D1), but these
  transcripts do not show Manual-mode prompts. Sessions 1–2 (2026-11-08) used the default config profile; later sessions the clean one.
- Material choices went to the owner (OD1–OD21 in the framework).

**Deviation from the agreed form** (framing Q14): there is no Claude Code hook example. The framework
defines no specific hook, and hooks fail open unless set to block (framework layer 2); `allowManagedHooksOnly` is in the managed
settings example instead (owner decision, [work/05-deliverable-plan.md](work/05-deliverable-plan.md) §5 Q6).

## Transcripts

All Claude Code sessions for this challenge were run in this repository. The sessions of
2026-11-08 up to session 2 used the default profile (`~/.claude`); later sessions use a clean profile (`~/.claude-papaya`, see
[work/setup-clean-config.sh](work/setup-clean-config.sh)). Each session is one
`<session-id>.jsonl` file plus an optional `<session-id>/` directory holding subagent
transcripts and large tool results (📖 [Claude directory reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-directory#cleaned-up-automatically)).
They are copied, unedited, into [transcripts/](transcripts/) before each commit that ends a session:

```bash
for CFG in ~/.claude ~/.claude-papaya; do
  SRC="$CFG/projects/-home-do-hoang-minh-hung-papaya-devsecops-challenge"
  [ -d "$SRC" ] && rsync -a --exclude='memory/' --include='*.jsonl' --include='*/' --include='*/**' "$SRC"/ transcripts/
done
```

Claude Code deletes local transcripts after `cleanupPeriodDays` (default 30 days, minimum 1,
cannot be disabled). Both profiles on the machine used for this challenge set it to 365 days.

46	|---|---|
47	| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
48	| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |

50	| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |

52	**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**
53	
54	- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
55	  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
56	  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
57	  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
58	- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
59	  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
60	- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
61	  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
62	  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
63	- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
64	  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
65	  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
66	  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
67	- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
68	  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
69	  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
70	  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
71	  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
72	  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
73	  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
74	  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
75	- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
76	  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
77	  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
78	  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
79	  for speed.
80	- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no CloudTrail for k0s changes
81	  (so S3 reconciliation does not cover them), and no break-glass when Actions is down (G1, G2).
82	- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
83	  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
84	  unavailable" for JIT. Their keys and hosting are open (G19).
85	- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
86	  business associate, as the brief implies.
87	
88	**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):
89	
90	1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
91	   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
92	2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
93	3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
94	4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.

110	## Layer 1 — Identity and access
111	
112	**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
113	written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
114	to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.
115	
116	**On Papaya's stack**
117

119	  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
120	  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
121	  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
122	  holds.
123	- **Process rules** that follow from this:
124	  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
125	    accepted as a process control, D2);
126	  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
127	    research 6.9.4 Q2);
128	  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
129	  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
130	    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
131	    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
132	    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
133	    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no

136	  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim

278	## Layer 3 — Change workflow by risk level
279	
280	**Principle.** The level is set by the damage a change can do. One default path above non-prod: a
281	reviewed PR applied by the pipeline, with the JIT fallback (layer 7) as the only other write path.
282	The approver reviews the code change that will be applied. Every prod change needs two people, and
283	no more by default: one who makes it and one who approves it; the on-call backup only replaces an
284	unavailable primary (OD2). Higher risk narrows **who** may approve (the owners of that path), not how
285	many. Separately, any prod diff that looks risky stops the deploy, whatever its level; that adds a
286	second approval by an owner of the same stack, which keeps it to two people (OD8). Confirmed by the owner
287	(OD13): the original author opens the approval PR and the first approver
288	approves it. If the first approver is unavailable, another owner of the stack approves; that makes
289	three people and is recorded as a deviation, counted monthly (OD11). A cross-team PR needs one
290	approval, as GitHub accepts one on-call group member for files of several owner teams (OD10,
291	OD9, 📖 R3.2.7); domain review there is a recommendation, counted in the monthly report. A real-data read is not a change and has its own rule, L3-data. Incidents use the same
292	path with faster people, not fewer security checks.
293	
294	| Level | What | Examples | Approval | Path |
295	|---|---|---|---|---|
296	| **L0** | Read: non-prod anything; prod metadata | metrics, redacted logs | none | read-only identity |
297	| **L1** | Change in non-prod | deploy a branch to dev; `pulumi preview` on non-prod (needs state-write permission on a DIY S3 backend, 📖 R4.3.3) | author only | non-prod roles or PR pipeline |

L3 paths (workflow and agent-config files, catalogue, the SCP stack): the L3 owner team only (OD13); IAM-only stacks are deployable, so the L3 owner team plus the on-call group (OD9). L3 content inside a domain file (an IAM statement in `serverless.yml`, a stateful delete): the stack's owner, then the risk stop (OD8). In incidents: the on-call approver for deployable paths (OD9); paths that define the process (CODEOWNERS, agent config, catalogue, workflows) wait for the L3 owner team | same path; for IaC changes the risk stop also applies; workflow and agent-config files have no prod diff |
300	| **L3-JIT** | Break-glass | ECS force-redeploy while Actions is down | on-call approver ≠ requester (Options §4b); incidents only, as the owner accepted it (Options §9 Q2); the on-call approver counts as owner of the service in the request (OD13) | layer 7 |
301	| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |

303	`CLAUDE.md` and the other agent configuration files are L3, because they define the workflow for
304	the whole team (OD3). With code-owner review on, every PR, L2 included, needs an approval from an
305	owner of the files it touches (📖 R3.2.3, R3.2.7; per-file behaviour ⚠️ not a separate research row).
306	What differs at L3 is **which team** owns the path: L3 paths are owned in CODEOWNERS by a designated
307	L3 owner team (deployable L3 paths also by the on-call group, OD9), L2 paths by their domain team; and IaC changes at L3 meet the
308	risk stop. Most IAM, network and stateful changes sit inside domain files, so they are approved by

310	`check-no-new-access` (📖 R2.8.1) and the Pulumi policy pack (📖 R4.2.2), both from phase 2 (layer 5). Cost: changes to `CLAUDE.md` (where D3 puts shared knowledge) need the L3 owner team, not
311	the domain team that edits it most.

314	
315	- **Gate = merge to `main`.** On Team, environment reviewers do not exist for private repos
316	  (📖 R3.1.2). Ruleset on `main`: PR required, 1 approval, code-owner review, dismiss stale approvals,
317	  approval by someone other than the last pusher, required checks from a pinned source app, no force
318	  push, empty bypass list (📖 R3.2.2, R3.2.3, R3.2.5). Branch up to date before merge, since there is

322	  group would not satisfy at night, and how it combines several teams is not researched (⚠️), so it

A required check with a pinned source app (📖 R3.2.5), set by a dedicated GitHub App that reacts to review events and is the pinned source [design; hosting, key storage and whether its key counts against S2 are not researched, ⚠️ G19], adds what
324	  the rules cannot: for app-opened PRs it excludes the person who triggered the agent, and it counts

388	- **Incident lane:** label `incident`, on-call approver paged, security checks always run (S10), only

392	**Example: Lambda timeouts at 2 a.m.** (Options §6)
393	
394	The incident responder is engineer E; the on-call approver is R (a backup replaces R only if R is
395	unavailable).
396	
397	1. E's incident-analysis session reads metrics and redacted logs and proposes `timeout` 30 → 90 s,
398	   memory 1024 → 2048 MB, and a larger visibility timeout on the source queue (ratio ⚠️ Options §8).
399	2. A second session (edit tools; not meant to use prod roles) edits `serverless.yml`, runs
400	   `serverless diff` on non-prod, and opens a PR labelled `incident` as E.
401	3. R, a co-owner of `serverless.yml` through the on-call group (OD9), reviews the diff. If R
402	   catches a missing queue change, R does not fix it (OD7): E pushes the fix, the stale approval is
403	   dismissed, and R approves again, one more review round (Options §6). E merges.
404	4. The deploy workflow packages, previews prod, finds no risky change, deploys with the OIDC role.
405	5. Estimate 11–46 min (⚠️ Options §6) against ≤ 30 min: measured first in rollout.
406	
407	**Audit evidence.** The PR (diff, approvers, checks), the deploy run log and risk-stop summary (exported, retention ⚠️ G7), the `deploy-approvals/` PR, and CloudTrail events linked by commit SHA and run ID; walk-through: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#evidence-for-one-prod-change-s8).

410	usually by the same approver, when the risk stop fires (OD13; OD11). Cross-team PRs: one approval (OD10). None in non-prod.
411	Compliance gets four-eyes enforced by GitHub. Gap: on Team the prod diff is not seen before apply.

450	## Layer 5 — CI/CD hardening
451	
452	**Principle.** CI is the default production writer, so it is the main target. Short-lived,
453	least-privilege credentials per job. Every CI dependency is pinned. Agent-written code passes the same
454	checks as human code (S10).
455	
456	**On Papaya's stack**
457	
458	- **Credentials:** OIDC instead of keys and tokens in repository secrets, which any writer can read
459	  (📖 R3.4.1, R3.5.3b). Org default for `GITHUB_TOKEN` set to "restricted", `permissions:` per job (📖 R3.5.3).
460	  "Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests" off (📖 R3.3.3). Serverless License Key in
461	  SSM, read by the deploy role (sf ≥ 4.4.19, 📖 R4.4.8). Until G1/G2 are solved, k0s and Firebase
462	  deploys may need a stored credential in GitHub: a kubeconfig or token for k0s, a Firebase token or
463	  service-account key for Firebase Hosting. The owner accepts this as an exception to S2 = 0 until it
464	  is checked whether k0s and Firebase deploys can use OIDC (OD1, OD6). Conditions [design]:
465	  - stored only as an **environment secret of `production`**, never as a repository secret. Anyone
466	    with write access can read repository secrets (📖 R3.5.3b), which would turn the exception into
467	    standing prod write for every engineer and their agent. Environment secrets and a deployment
468	    branch rule limited to `main` are available on Team for private repos (📖 R3.1.2, R3.1.3), and
469	    only the reviewed deploy workflow references the environment (layer 3);
470	  - the deploy job runs on GitHub-hosted runners. On self-hosted runners, jobs "are not run in an
471	    isolated container, even if they use environments", so environment secrets there must be
472	    treated like repository secrets (📖 R3.1.5). Self-hosted runners "can be persistently
473	    compromised by untrusted code" from anyone who can open a PR, and runner groups limit only which
474	    repositories use them (📖 R3.5.2); in a monorepo any workflow can likely target the runner's label (⚠️ G15).
475	    How to restrict a runner to one workflow is not researched (⚠️ G15); just-in-time runners exist
476	    (📖 R3.5.2, not read in detail). If reaching k0s needs a self-hosted runner, that
477	    runner is dedicated to the `production` deploy, and the residual risk is recorded;
478	  - that environment secret is the single source of truth: no copy elsewhere (OD1);
479	  - an owner, an expiry and rotation in the exception register;
480	  - optionally a separate environment (e.g. `production-k0s`), limited to `main` and referenced
481	    only by the k0s/Firebase deploy workflow, so AWS deploy jobs cannot read these secrets
482	    [design].
483	
484	  Residual risk: admins can change the environment, and a deleted environment comes back without
485	  protection (⚠️ R3.1.4); the alerts and settings comparison in layer 7 cover this. The exception
486	  covers **CI deploy credentials only**. Runtime credentials, such as a k0s autoscaler's AWS access to
487	  add or remove nodes, live in the cluster, not in GitHub; they follow layer 1 (no static keys, a
488	  role attached to the machine; ⚠️ not researched for k0s, G1).
489	- **Side paths:** Pulumi ESC, Pulumi Deployments and Serverless Dashboard providers reach AWS
490	  (📖 R4.4.9) outside the GitHub gate (⚠️ R4.4.9); not used for prod (⚠️ R4.6 #6).
491	- **Pinning:** workflow lockfile (`gh actions-lock`) or full SHA, enforced by the org policy "Require
492	  actions to be pinned to a full-length commit SHA" (availability on Team ⚠️); the lockfile does not pin reusable workflows, so

494	- **CODEOWNERS** on `.github/`, `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, `.claude/`, `.claude.json`, `.mcp.json`,

499	  `deploy-approvals/<stack>/`, owned by the stack's owners and the on-call group (OD8, OD9). The private plugin

535	## Layer 6 — Data protection and prompt-injection defence
536	
537	**Principle.** The design keeps PHI from reaching the coding agent (owner decision, research 1.9).
538	Some paths rely on process (below), so this is a target, not a guarantee. Other customer
539	personal data is outside that hard boundary ("not extended", research 5.8): the agent reads metadata
540	by default and may read such data case by case under GĐ-9. Real-data reads are approved, name one
541	tenant, are time-boxed, and need an agreement (BAA/DPA, partner contract) (GĐ-9). Everything read
542	from outside is untrusted. Non-prod is synthetic or masked (GĐ-14).
543	
544	**On Papaya's stack**
545	
546	- **Paths to PHI** (research 1.11.4 lists 17):
547	  - AWS stores: closed by identity, through `ProdReadMetadata` as the only standing prod role from
548	    phase 1 (existing broad read roles are removed) and the SCP from phase 2
549	    (layer 1); no Aurora credentials, no prod exec, no `lambda:InvokeFunction` for agent-usable roles
550	    [design; actions ⚠️ G13];
551	  - k0s logs/exec and GCP stores (L1, L11, L13): same principle, mechanism open (G1, G3);
552	  - tickets/chat via MCP, pasted text, internal admin pages, prod AI traces, fixtures, CI logs (L5,
553	    L8–L10, L12, L14): process and hygiene only;
554	  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
555	- **Real-data request** [design]: tenant, purpose, store, window, agreement; approved by the data owner
556	  and an approver ≠ requester; JIT data-read role, 1 h. At night the data owner is not on call: the
557	  on-call approver approves alone and the data owner reviews the grant the next working day. This
558	  applies to non-PHI and PHI alike; for PHI the reader is still a human without an agent. Per-tenant scoping through session tags
559	  (📖 R2.1.8) is unresolved, because tags come from user attributes (⚠️).
560	  - **PHI:** a human reads in a terminal without an agent (process rule, layer 1); the agent gets a
561	    redacted summary. This
562	    narrows GĐ-9 because the agent stays outside PHI scope (research 1.9) and Team is not shown as
563	    BAA-covered (⚠️ R1.11.3.4). Enterprise + BAA only for a separate environment if needed (research 1.9).
564	  - **Non-PHI personal data:** the agent may read it within the approved request (GĐ-9). Claim
565	    tables mix health, ID and bank data (research 1.11.4 L2), so a store that holds PHI is treated as
566	    PHI unless the agent reads a view or extract without PHI [design].
567	- **Partner-uploaded claim documents (A7b):** never in an agent session raw; reproduce with synthetic
568	  documents, or de-identify first [design]. The document is PHI and an injection vector (research
569	  1.11.4 L6).
570	- **Injection** (these lower frequency; layers 1 and 3 limit impact): Manual by default (sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, layer 2); the auto-mode
571	  classifier missed 17 % of 52 real overeager actions and 5.7 % of 1,000 synthetic exfiltration
572	  attempts (📖 R6.3.5). Broad allowed domains such as `github.com` are a documented exfiltration path
573	  (📖 R6.3.7). The incident session has no WebFetch, likely no edit tools (layer 2), and runs outside
574	  the repo, but its Bash can still write locally and send data out through excluded
575	  commands (layer 2), including the SSO token cache; "no standing write, no PHI read" limits what
576	  the token opens, except during a JIT or data-read window (layer 2 mitigations). Shared knowledge
577	  goes in `CLAUDE.md` under review; auto memory is exempt from the protected-path rules unless `--restricted` (📖 R6.3.11, D3).
578	- **Tenants:** one tenant per data-read grant; a session that read one tenant's data does not post to
579	  shared places without review (⚠️ R6.5 #8, process). Logical separation in shared accounts is assumed
580	  (GĐ-3, unconfirmed).
581	- **Non-prod:** no prod copies (S11). A scan of non-prod stores runs at the start of phase 1 (tool:
582	  G4); a store not yet scanned follows the L3-data rule (GĐ-14: until cleaned, non-prod follows the GĐ-9 data-read rule). Cost: until scanned, that store is
583	  not part of the free loop.
584	- **Local stores:** transcripts and memory hold what the agent read (research 1.11.4); set
585	  `cleanupPeriodDays` (30 in the HIPAA sample, 📖 R5.5.4; what it deletes ⚠️).
586	- **Cross-border (Vietnam example):** processing data collected in Vietnam on a platform abroad is a
587	  transfer (📖 R5.4.5); agent flows, including employee names in logs and transcripts, update the
588	  transfer impact assessment (⚠️ R5.7 #4, needs Papaya legal).
589	
590	**Audit evidence.** SCP/IAM text as the written access rule for sensitive data, real-data requests with the data-read role's CloudTrail events, and non-prod scan results; full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).
591	
592	**Cost / value.** Debugging with redacted and synthetic data; a request for the rare real-data read.
593	Compliance gets "minimum necessary" (📖 R1.11.1.8) enforced by IAM for AWS stores (fully from phase 2;
594	actions ⚠️ G13) and by process
595	elsewhere, and a record per exception (S9).
596	
597	---
598	
599	## Layer 7 — Observability, audit, incident response and break-glass
600	
601	**Principle.** One tamper-evident evidence chain per prod change. One routed alert channel with a
602	named on-call, approvers included. Unapproved change is detected (drift, reconciliation). Break-glass
603	is approved before use, time-boxed and reconciled after.
604	
605	**On Papaya's stack**
606	
607	- **Audit stores:**
608	  - organization CloudTrail to a log-archive account with integrity validation (📖 R2.6.2, R2.6.4,
609	    R2.6.5); change records ≥ 6 years; raw-log retention for Papaya's compliance owner (⚠️ R5.7 #2).
610	    Data events only on PHI buckets, prod Lambda invoke and prod SQS (cost 📖 R2.6.3; selection
611	    ⚠️ R2.9 #5), which makes the archive
612	    PHI-bearing (⚠️ research 1.11.4 L15). CloudTrail Lake is closed to new customers (📖 R2.6.6);
613	  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days, so exported (📖 R3.5.6);
614	  - alerts on `repository_ruleset.update`, `environment.update_protection_rule`,
615	    `environment.remove_protection_rule`, `environment.delete`, `protected_branch.policy_override`
616	    (📖 R3.5.6, R3.1.4; selection ⚠️ R3.6 #1). UI changes to the branch policy may leave no event, and a
617	    deleted `production` environment comes back unprotected (⚠️ R3.1.4): a job compares live settings
618	    with an expected copy (G8);
619	  - Aurora SQL is likely invisible to CloudTrail (⚠️ R2.7.1): Database Activity Streams, alerts on
620	    lost-record events (📖 R2.7.2; Serverless v2 ⚠️), stream treated as PHI (⚠️ R2.7.3);
621	  - Claude Code OTel without prompt content (layer 2).
622	- **Change record [design]:** keyed by commit SHA or JIT request ID; links PR, approvals, run ID,
623	  preview and CloudTrail events. Monthly reconciliation: every prod write event matches a record
624	  approved before apply (S3). Actor: `onBehalfOf.userId` where present, else session name plus
625	  directory lookup (📖 R2.5.1; ⚠️ R2.5.3).
626	- **Drift [design]:** its own role, trusted only from a `drift` environment on `main`; it can read
627	  prod secrets in state, which is noted (⚠️ R4.6 #2). Scheduled `pulumi preview --refresh
628	  --expect-no-changes` or `pulumi refresh --preview-only` (📖 R4.1.1, R4.3.1, R4.3.2). On a DIY S3
629	  backend, preview needs state-write permission (📖 R4.3.3); whether a refresh preview writes more
630	  than locks is open (⚠️ R4.6 #2, G14). So either the drift role gets state write (and the same
631	  trust care as the deploy role), or Pulumi Cloud drift detection is used (📖 R4.3.2, Pro+). The
632	  latter runs on Pulumi Deployments, which holds credentials to prod, so it re-opens a side path that
633	  layer 5 excludes and needs the same trust narrowing and audit (📖 R4.4.9; ⚠️ R4.6 #6). CloudFormation
634	  drift detection, explicitly set properties only (📖 R4.4.6). No auto-remediation: it is an unreviewed
635	  `pulumi up --refresh` (📖 R4.3.2). Each finding gets an actor and a ticket.
636	- **On-call:** phase 1 delivers the named approver schedule (primary + backup engineers, 24/7), as
637	  decided in framing round 1, and, because of OD7, a minimal incident-responder schedule; the
638	  latter extends that decision. The primary approves; the backup steps in only if the primary is
639	  unavailable (OD2). On-call approvers only approve during their shift; the fix is written by an
640	  incident responder (OD7). Alert routing and the
641	  rest of on-call follow in phase 2 (tools: G5); in phase 1 the responder calls the approver by phone from the published schedule.
642	- **Break-glass = JIT fallback** [design unless marked]:
643	
644	  | Step | Rule |
645	  |---|---|
646	  | When | Only during an incident (Options §9 Q2), when the PR path cannot be used: operation not in IaC and no runbook; GitHub/Actions down; pipeline broken. The approver refuses JIT for anything expressible in IaC while the pipeline works, and records why. Outside incidents, an operation not in IaC waits for IaC or a runbook. |
647	  | Request | Command list, scope, reason, incident link, in a channel that does not depend on GitHub. |
648	  | Approval | On-call approver ≠ requester, before the grant (Options §4b; OD7; backup rule OD2). |
649	  | Grant | `InfraOperator-<service>`; role session 1 h (📖 R2.1.4). Deleting the assignment likely stops only new sessions (⚠️ R2.4.2, R2.9 #3), so the real window can approach 2 h; ending the portal session does not end role sessions (📖 R2.4.3). An immediate stop needs the revocation SCP, which must keep the user blocked for at least 12 h (📖 R2.4.4). Applying it is a management-account change held by the L3 owner team only, and no night-time path for it is designed yet (⚠️ G20): until one exists, a misused grant may run to the end of its window. Candidate: a pre-approved revocation runbook for one named L3 owner reachable by phone, or an org-wide `aws:TokenIssueTime` Deny as kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3). |
650	  | Execution | The grant goes to the requester (the incident responder), who types the commands; no agent in that terminal (D2). D2 said the on-call person runs them; OD7 moves that to the responder, since on-call engineers only approve. |
651	  | After | A job compares CloudTrail writes in the window with the list; a codify PR within a fixed deadline (as soon as GitHub is back); drift detection until it merges. |
652	  | Identity Center outage | Emergency SAML federation to roles, built and tested in advance (📖 R2.1.11; ⚠️ R2.9 #2); no user mapped until an approved activation, which is alerted. |
653	
654	  **Example request (illustrative command ⚠️):** "INC-123, ECS service `claims-api`, Actions outage. Run
655	  `aws ecs update-service --cluster <prod-cluster> --service <svc> --force-new-deployment`. Scope
656	  `InfraOperator-claims`, 1 h."
657	
658	  **Metrics** (Options §7; starting thresholds ⚠️ to calibrate): JIT used where a PR was possible
659	  (review at 1); writes outside the list (review at 1); codify PRs late (review at 1); grants per
660	  month and share of incidents needing non-IaC operations (review above about 25 %, a value new in
661	  this draft). On a breach,
662	  make the PR lane faster or add a runbook; do not widen JIT.
663	- **Roadmap:** runbooks for repeated non-IaC operations, if SSM Automation's approval step meets three
664	  conditions (Options §2; outside 02-research, G6); break-glass from an environment without the agent
665	  (D2, ⚠️).
666	
667	**Audit evidence.** Validated CloudTrail, the exported GitHub audit log, change records and monthly reconciliation (S3, S8), JIT records, drift tickets and incident approval waits (S7); full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).
668	
669	**Cost / value.** The incident lane is slower than direct access (estimated 11–46 vs 2–20 min,
670	Options §6), and JIT needs a written command list. Compliance gets approval before apply even in
671	incidents, plus detection.
672	
673	---
674	
675	## Layer 8 — Governance and rollout
676	
677	**Principle.** Every control has an owner, a metric and a review date. Policies are files changed by
678	PR. Access is never removed before its replacement works. Controls are tested against realistic
679	attacks.
680	
681	**On Papaya's stack**
682	
683	- **Owners:** DevSecOps (framework, managed settings, catalogue, metrics); a platform team or named
684	  engineers (deploy workflows, rulesets, pipelines; whether Papaya has a platform team is unknown ⚠️); Compliance (evidence review, supplier register, Statement of
685	  Applicability); engineering leads (decide CODEOWNERS content; changes to it are approved by the L3 owner team); engineering management (on-call schedule).
686	- **Policy as code:** catalogue, SCPs, trust policies, CODEOWNERS and workflows are files under
687	  CODEOWNERS. Settings that live outside files are kept as an expected copy in git and compared with
688	  the live state: GitHub settings (⚠️ R3.6 #1; G8) and Claude managed settings, which are edited in
689	  the admin console (📖 R1.1.5; comparison method in layer 2). Few GitHub admins and Claude org
690	  Owners, reviewed quarterly.
691	- **Metrics:** S1–S11 exactly as in framing §5; this framework adds the JIT metrics (layer 7) and the
692	  prompt metrics (layer 2). S2 and S5 have caveats (OD1; layer 2).
693	- **Rollout** (≈ 90 days, GĐ-12 unconfirmed): [`03-rollout-plan.md`](03-rollout-plan.md), moved
694	  there with its items unchanged except syncs with the examples' findings (trail deny, allowlist,
695	  phase-2 version floor), and expanded with owners and checks [design]. Order (framing Q8): (1) remove long-lived CI credentials, (2) narrow standing prod
696	  access, (3) MCP/plugin catalogue; the on-call approver list before or with (2). Phase 1 (0–30 days)
697	  makes the PR the default prod write path, with six hard prerequisites before standing prod write is
698	  removed; phase 2 (30–60) adds SCPs, the rest of the managed baseline and automated
699	  reconciliation; phase 3 (60–90) tests and reviews. The phase-1 load on 1–2 DevSecOps people is the
700	  main rollout risk [design; effort not estimated ⚠️].
701	
702	- **Exceptions:** a ticket with owner, reason and expiry.
703	- **Standards mapping:** ISO 27001:2022 Annex A (IDs recalled, ⚠️ R5.1), HIPAA Security Rule
704	  (📖 R5.2) and Vietnam law (📖 R5.4) are mapped per control area in the
705	  [compliance register](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference), with every caveat. "A named human approves"
706	  is Papaya's chosen way to meet these controls, not a literal requirement (⚠️ R5.7 #1).
707	- **Out of scope:** security of the production AI agents (A7a); noted as a follow-up.
708	
709	**Audit evidence.** Git history of policy files, monthly metrics, 90-day review minutes, the exception register and planted-injection reports; standards: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#standards-cross-reference).
710	
711	**Cost / value.** Steady, small overhead for DevSecOps and the owners of deploy workflows. Compliance gets a managed system
712	with owners and review dates.
713	
714	---
715	
716	## Gaps (not covered, or only as an open item, in `work/02-research.md`)
717	
718	| # | Gap | Layers |
719	|---|---|---|
720	| G1 | k0s: authentication, RBAC, audit logging, kubeconfig issuance (GĐ-4); break-glass when Actions is down | 1, 3, 6, 7 |
721	| G2 | Firebase Hosting deploy from CI without a stored token; break-glass when Actions is down | 1, 5, 7 |
722	| G3 | Human and agent access to GCP (roles, data access) | 1, 6 |
723	| G4 | Secret scanning, dependency check, SAST, non-prod data scanning on the Team plan | 5, 6 |
724	| G5 | Paging and alert routing; approving a PR from a phone | 7 |
725	| G6 | SSM Automation `aws:approve` (read in `work/03-options.md` §2, not in 02-research) | 7 |
726	| G7 | GitHub Actions log and artifact retention, and export | 3, 7 |
727	| G8 | Rulesets and environment settings through the API | 7, 8 |
728	| G9 | How Linear and Slack MCP servers authenticate | 4, 6 |
729	| G10 | OIDC subject customisation (`job_workflow_ref`) on GitHub Team | 1 |
730	| G11 | Closing provider/login bypasses on laptops without MDM | 2 |
731	| G12 | `pulumi up` flag reference for the prod allowlist | 3 |
732	| G13 | IAM actions for every data-plane read (S3, SQS, Step Functions, Secrets Manager, RDS, ECS Exec, Lambda invoke) | 1, 6 |
733	| G14 | Which state writes a Pulumi refresh preview needs on a DIY S3 backend | 3, 7 |
734	| G15 | Restricting a self-hosted runner to one workflow in a monorepo; just-in-time runners | 5 |
735	| G16 | Managing GitHub team membership as code; audit event for a membership change | 3, 7 |
736	| G17 | Who forms the L3 owner team and how many people (GĐ-1: never a single reviewer) | 3, 8 |
737	| G18 | Reading the live values of server-managed settings (API or local cache) to compare with git | 2, 8 |
738	| G19 | Required-check app and CI-agent app: review-event triggers, source pinning against same-name checks, hosting, private-key storage and whether those keys count against S2; the app's check that a risk-stop approval matches the stopped run's hash (OD18) | 3, 5 |
739	| G20 | Emergency revocation at night: who can apply the revocation Deny SCP (management account) within minutes; `aws:TokenIssueTime` kill switch (⚠️ R2.9 #3) | 1, 7 |
740	
741	Open checks from `work/03-options.md` §8 remain open.
742	
743	## Owner decisions (2026-11-09)
744	
745	The owner answered the open questions of draft v3. English rendering; the original Vietnamese
746	answers are recorded in `work/session-log.md`.
747	
748	| # | Question | Decision |
749	|---|---|---|
750	| OD1 | Exception to S2 = 0 for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials? | Yes, provided each credential has a single source of truth. (The first reason given, continuous scale-in/scale-out, concerns runtime credentials; OD6 narrowed the scope.) |
751	| OD2 | L3: must one approver be from the platform team? | Not necessarily; one approval procedure is agreed for all engineers, and the on-call engineer is enough. Clarified in follow-ups: every change involves two people, one who makes it and one who approves; the on-call backup only replaces an unavailable primary. Asked whether L3 should need more approvers than L2, the owner chose "L3 = 1 approver at all times"; in the agent's framing of that option, the approver must own the path. |
752	| OD3 | `CLAUDE.md` changes: L2 or L3? | L3, because the workflow must be consistent across the whole team. |
753	| OD4 | Move the rest of the managed baseline and the SSM check to phase 2? | Yes. |
754	| OD5 | "An agent does not approve PRs" only a process rule? | It is a rule: the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent. |
755	| OD6 | Scope of OD1: CI deploy credentials only, or also runtime scaling credentials? | CI deploy credentials (k0s kubeconfig/token, Firebase token in GitHub secrets) only, until it is checked whether k0s and Firebase can use OIDC. |
756	| OD7 | (a) If the on-call engineer writes an L3 fix, who approves? (b) Keep the read-only allowlist in phase 1? | (a) "While on call, never change the process"; clarified: on-call engineers only approve, and fixes are written by another engineer (the incident responder), so the approver is never the author. (b) Yes, as proposed. |
757	| OD8 | IAM/network/stateful changes inside a domain file: who approves the risk stop? | The stack's owners (may be the first approver); always two people. The L3 owner team keeps only the real L3 paths; Access Analyzer and policy packs compensate. |
758	| OD9 | How can one on-call primary approve any path at night? | The on-call approver group co-owns every deployable path; one primary + one backup. Normal-day domain review is a process rule with a monthly check. |
759	| OD10 | A PR touching files of several domain teams: split, or one approval? | One approval is enough (two-person rule kept); domain review on such PRs is a recommendation, counted in the monthly report. |
760	| OD11 | Risk stop when the first approver is unavailable: may another owner of the stack approve? | Yes; it makes three people and is recorded as a deviation. |
761	| OD12 | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed`: `true` or `false`? | Keep `true` (fewer prompts, relies on the sandbox, which arrives in phase 2). |
762	| OD13 | Confirm three agent readings: (1) OD8, who opens and approves the risk-stop approval PR; (2) OD9, scope of the on-call group; (3) L3-JIT, does the on-call approver count as service owner? | Confirmed: (1) the original author opens it and the first approver approves it; (2) the on-call group does not co-own process-defining paths or the SCP stack, which only the L3 owner team approves; (3) yes. |
763	| OD14 | Add the risk-stop classifier (`tools/risk-stop/`) to the canonical L3 path list? (found while writing `examples/`) | Yes: it is a control, so only the L3 owner team may change it. |
764	| OD15 | Scope of the risk stop: risky diffs nobody looked at, or also malicious approved code? | Keep the current scope and state its limits; a separate prod preview role and a job split go to the phase-2 roadmap. |
765	| OD16 | Squash-only merges to `main` (needed so a PR cannot carry its own risk-stop approval)? | Yes; the cost is that PR-internal commit history is not kept on `main`. |
766	| OD17 | Deploy only the current tip of `main`, so re-running an old run cannot roll prod back? | Yes; added to the layer-3 "merge approval = deploy approval" conditions. |
767	| OD18 | An approval merged before a deploy stops, matched by a later change outside the stack's directory, is still accepted | Accepted as a stated limit; the approval-gate app (G19) is to close it by checking the stopped run's hash. |
768	| OD19 | Protect the names of SCP-exempt roles (`app-claims-*`, `cfn-deployment-*`, `github-prod-deploy-*`) so that only the IAM stack's deploy role can create or change them? (found while writing `examples/`) | Yes. Confirmed reading: "only the IAM stack" holds once OD20 gives the IAM stack its own role and OIDC subject; until then the protection is "only an approved prod Pulumi deploy". |
769	| OD20 | Code in the deploy job (install scripts, Pulumi program, Serverless plugins) can request the job's OIDC token for either prod deploy role: fix now or roadmap? | Roadmap phase 2, together with OD15: a build job without `id-token`, and per-role environments (different OIDC subjects) or `job_workflow_ref`. Until then it is a stated limit. |
770	| OD21 | Phase 1 lets built-in read-only commands (`cat`, `head` …) read `~/.aws` without a prompt, and allow rules skip the auto-mode classifier: add keys to the phase-1 subset? | Yes: add a `Read(~/.aws/**)` deny rule and `autoMode.classifyAllShell: true` (examples finding 19). |

# Framework: coding agents for DevSecOps at Papaya

> Status: v3 after 17 independent review rounds; approved by the owner 2026-11-09 · Updated: 2026-11-09
> Audience: a panel of Engineering and Compliance. Each layer ends with what it costs engineers and
> what it gives Compliance.

## How to read this

Eight layers. Each has a **Principle** (tool-independent), **On Papaya's stack** (Pulumi,
Serverless Framework, GitHub Actions, AWS, GCP, k0s, Claude Code) and **Audit evidence** (records an
auditor can test without asking anyone). Copy-paste detail belongs in `examples/`.

| Marker | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 📖 R*x.y* | Documented. R*x.y* is a ✅/📖 row in `work/02-research.md` that quotes or links the official page (a few rows cite vendor blogs, bulletins or example files instead, e.g. R2.4.1b, R6.3.5, R5.5.4). |
| ⚠️ R*x.y* | Inference, open question or "What this means for Papaya" conclusion in the research (sections 1.8, 2.9, 3.6, 3.7, 4.6, 5.6, 5.7, 6.5), or the ⚠️ part of a mixed row. Reasoned, not documented. |
| ⚠️ | Not verified at all, e.g. an illustrative command. |
| [design] | My proposal, built from documented parts, untested. Treat as ⚠️. |
| 📖 + inline link | Official page linked in place, or in the cited examples finding / E-row: facts found while writing `examples/` (2026-11-09), after the research file. |

This is a design without access to Papaya's systems; nothing was run against them. The files in
[`examples/`](../examples/README.md) were checked locally (✅, commands and output there), and
"examples finding n" / "E*n*" point to that file.
**GĐ-n** = assumption in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §4 (owner-confirmed: GĐ-1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11,
14; the others are marked "unconfirmed" where used); **S-n** = success criteria
(§5); **P/A-n** = problems (§1); **D1–D3** = owner decisions in research 6.6; **Options §n** =
`work/03-options.md`; **G-n** = gaps; **OD-n** = owner decisions on this draft (both at the end).
Earlier owner answers are cited with their source: "research 6.9.4 Q4", "framing Q8", "Options §9 Q2".

---

## 1. The decision in one page

Engineering and Compliance disagree only about **writes to production**; reads of metadata and all
of non-prod are outside Compliance's sentence (framing §3.1). Real customer data is layer 6.

**Chosen approach "A + D2'"** (Options §9, owner decision 2026-11-09):

1. **Default path:** every prod change is a pull request, approved by a named human who is not the
   author, applied by CI. Incidents included ("IaC first").
2. **Fallback (break-glass):** only when the PR path cannot be used, a human gets an approved grant
   with a 1-hour role session (effective window up to about 2 h, ⚠️ R2.9 #3) and runs an approved command list in a terminal without an agent (layer 7) [design].
3. **Nothing standing:** no human or agent holds standing prod write; no long-lived credentials.

| Engineering gets | Compliance gets |
|---|---|
| A free loop in non-prod: read, change, deploy without approval (non-prod is synthetic or masked, GĐ-14; stores not yet scanned are excluded, layer 6). | Every prod change approved **before** apply by a named human ≠ author (GĐ-8, GĐ-11), enforced in GitHub and AWS IAM, outside the agent (limits below). |
| Read-only prod metadata for the agent. | No standing prod write (S1), no long-lived CI keys (S2, with an owner-approved exception for k0s/Firebase deploy credentials, OD1, OD6; storage conditions [design], layer 5). |
| Self-service PRs, one approval, same-day ship (S4). | One evidence chain per change; approval and change records ≥ 6 years (📖 R5.2.9; applied to change records ⚠️ R5.7 #2). |
| Incident lane: approval wait ≤ 15 min, 24/7 (S7). Decision-to-apply target ≤ 30 min (Options §9); current estimate 11–46 min ⚠️, measured first in rollout. | Agent-side controls as a second layer, not the control of record. |

**Where the design falls short, stated openly:**

- **The fallback meets the approval rule only partly** (approves a command list, not an applied
  change); accepted by the owner (Options §9 Q2). It is a second, process-controlled path, while the
  framing asked for one technically enforced path (framing §3.3, Options §7). It stays narrow only
  if most incidents are expressible in IaC (unknown, Options §8); layer 7 measures this.
- **On GitHub Team nobody sees the prod diff before apply** (⚠️ R4.6 #1; Team assumed, GĐ-5).
  Risky prod diffs stop the deploy until an owner of the stack approves the prod preview [design].
- **Admins can edit the gate**; logged, not prevented (logging 📖 R3.2.2; ability to edit ⚠️ R3.2.2,
  R3.6 #1). An admin's agent has
  the same power, because the agent uses its engineer's GitHub login (⚠️ R6.5 #10).
- **Some rules are process, not technology:** see "Process rules" in layer 1. The owner's rule
  "the PR approver is always an engineer, never an agent" (OD5) is absolute as policy, but on
  laptops it is enforced by policy and training, not by a technical control: an agent could approve
  through its engineer's login, and no detection was found.
- **Incident approvers vs domain review:** code-owner review means an approver must own the file,
  at L2 as at L3. So that one on-call primary can approve any deployable path at 2 a.m., the on-call approver
  group co-owns every deployable path (owner decision OD9, layer 3). The cost: GitHub accepts an
  approval from any listed owner (📖 R3.2.7), so on normal days that group could approve another
  domain's PR. Domain review on normal days becomes a process rule with a monthly check, not a
  technical control. Because on-call approvers only
  approve (OD7), a night incident needs two people awake: the incident responder and the on-call
  approver (the backup only replaces an unavailable primary).
- **One approver for high-risk changes.** L3 changes (IAM, stateful deletes, workflow files) get one
  approver, like L2, but the path is owned by the L3 owner team (or by the stack's owners for L3
  content in domain files, OD8), and risky prod diffs stop for a look at
  the prod preview (OD2, OD8, layer 3). A single reviewer can miss things; this is the owner's trade-off
  for speed.
- **k0s and Firebase are weaker:** no prod preview or risk stop, no CloudTrail for k0s changes
  (so S3 reconciliation does not cover them), and no break-glass when Actions is down (G1, G2).
- **New dependencies on two GitHub Apps** (required check, CI agent): if the required-check app is
  down, every merge to `main` is blocked, incident PRs included; that counts as "pipeline
  unavailable" for JIT. Their keys and hosting are open (G19).
- **HIPAA applicability is a legal question** (⚠️ R1.11.1.11); the design treats Papaya as a
  business associate, as the brief implies.

**Cross-cutting rules** (owner's balance principle, research 6.8):

1. **The boundary is IAM and the CI gate.** Server-managed settings are "a client-side control, not
   a security boundary" (📖 R1.1.7); local admins can edit endpoint files (📖 R1.1.8).
2. **Assume prompt injection succeeds:** neither OWASP nor NIST knows a full prevention (📖 R6.1.1, R6.1.2).
3. **Friction where damage is large, none where it is small**, measured, with a time-boxed escape.
4. **Evidence by construction:** the path produces the records.

### Roles

| Role | Rule |
|---|---|
| Author (engineer + their agent) | Never approves own change; GitHub blocks PR authors from approving (📖 R3.3.1). |
| Approver | Always an engineer, never an agent (owner rule, OD5). Named in CODEOWNERS; ≠ author, ≠ last pusher (📖 R3.2.3); for an app-opened PR, ≠ the person who triggered it (⚠️ R3.3.4, layer 5). |
| Incident responder | Engineer who diagnoses and writes the fix or the JIT request. Never the on-call approver of the same shift (OD7). |
| On-call approver | Engineer on the on-call schedule, primary + backup, 24/7; wait ≤ 15 min (S7). While on call they only approve: they write no fix and file no JIT request, so the approver is always distinct from the author (OD7). The primary approves; the backup replaces an unavailable primary (OD2). No platform-team membership is required; all engineers follow one agreed approval procedure (OD2). |
| Data owner [design] | Named per tenant; co-approves real-data reads, or reviews a night-time read the next working day (layer 6). |
| Control owner | DevSecOps (1–2 people, GĐ-1); owns policies and metrics; not the only approver. |
| L3 owner team | Owns the process-defining L3 paths and the SCP stack (layer 3); composition open (G17). |

## Layer 1 — Identity and access

**Principle.** Every action traces to one named human. Nobody holds standing prod write: prod is
written by the pipeline role, or in the fallback by an approved, time-boxed grant. Prod reads default
to metadata. No long-lived credentials. Prod and non-prod are separate boundaries.

**On Papaya's stack**

- **The engineer's access is the agent's access.** The agent uses the engineer's AWS SSO cache, and
  one portal session reaches every role assigned to that engineer (📖 R2.2.1, R2.2.2; token-reuse
  detail ⚠️ R2.2.2). A separate
  "agent" permission set does not separate them (⚠️ R2.9 #1). The control is what the **engineer**
  holds.
- **Process rules** that follow from this:
  - the JIT terminal runs no agent, though the grant is reachable from the same laptop (owner
    accepted as a process control, D2);
  - the incident-analysis session is meant to use only read-only roles (D2; `--restricted` per D3,
    research 6.9.4 Q2);
  - the real-data terminal runs no agent when the store holds PHI [design], same weakness as D2;
  - an agent never approves PRs: an owner rule (OD5), enforced on laptops by policy and training.
    GitHub blocks self-approval only. The auto-mode default block list
    excerpt read names "approving Claude's own pull request" (📖 R6.3.3); whether approving
    someone else's PR is blocked is unverified (⚠️), and the list
    applies only in auto mode. No detection was found (⚠️; `actor_is_agent` in the audit log has no
    documented meaning, R3.5.6).
- **IAM Identity Center permission sets** (📖 R2.1.1) [design names]:
  - `ProdReadMetadata`: metrics, redacted log groups, configuration; no data-plane read on claim
    stores; 1 h session, the minimum (📖 R2.1.4). Some "metadata" reads (mostly ⚠️) return configuration or
    secrets, so `Resource: "*"` only for a reviewed action list (examples E6, findings 11, 12). Until a service's logs are redacted at source
    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only. Lambda configuration can hold secrets resolved by
    Serverless in plain text (⚠️ R4.4.7), so configuration reads are allowed per service only after
    its secrets move to runtime resolution (⚠️ R4.6 #7). Cost: until then the agent reads
    timeout/memory from the IaC code;
  - `NonProdDeveloper`: broad, non-prod accounts only;
  - `InfraOperator-<service>`: assigned only by the JIT flow (layer 7), via a partner product, the
    TEAM sample (📖 R2.4.1, R2.4.1b) or a small home-built flow (⚠️ R2.4.2) on the documented APIs
    `CreateAccountAssignment` / `DeleteAccountAssignment` (📖 R2.4.2);
  - no standing prod-write permission set.
- **SCPs on the prod OU** [design] (SCPs cap member-account principals, 📖 R2.3.1, R2.3.2):
  - deny data-plane reads on claim stores except application roles and the approved data-read role,
    by `aws:PrincipalArn` (📖 R2.3.8; pattern ⚠️ R2.9 #4). Actions, e.g. `s3:GetObject`,
    `sqs:ReceiveMessage`, `states:GetExecutionHistory`, are incomplete and unchecked (⚠️ G13);
  - deny `lambda:UpdateFunctionCode` / `lambda:UpdateFunctionConfiguration` (⚠️ R4.6 #3) except
    CloudFormation `deploymentRole`s, the Pulumi prod deploy role (if Pulumi manages Lambdas) and the
    JIT roles. The Serverless prod deploy role is a separate role and is not exempt: it only passes
    the `deploymentRole` (examples finding 13). This closes `serverless deploy function`, which changes config outside CloudFormation
    (📖 R4.4.4), and needs `deploymentRole` set on every Serverless stack (key 📖 R4.4.5; need ⚠️ R4.6 #3);
  - a pre-deployed revocation Deny on `identitystore:UserId` (📖 R2.4.4); deny changes to any trail
    in prod accounts, since member accounts cannot touch the organization trail anyway (📖 R2.6.2;
    examples findings 10, 15);
  - exempt role names are protected: only the IAM stack's deploy role may create or change such roles (OD19).
    Until OD20 gives the IAM stack its own role, that is the shared Pulumi prod deploy role, so in
    practice "only an approved prod Pulumi deploy" (examples finding 16).
  - Limits: 10 SCPs per target, 10,240 characters; no SCP applies to the management account
    (📖 R2.3.2, R2.3.4), so whatever deploys SCPs there is the most sensitive role (L3 path, held by the L3 owner team only, not co-owned by the on-call group; OD13).
- **Sessions/MFA:** portal session length set on purpose; an IdP session can extend it silently
  (📖 R2.1.5, R2.1.6). MFA lives in the external IdP if one is used (📖 R2.1.7).
- **CI → AWS:** GitHub OIDC, no stored keys (📖 R3.4.1). The prod role trusts only the `production`
  environment of the monorepo, in its `sub` format (📖 R3.4.3, R3.4.4; immutable format assumed,
  ⚠️ R3.7 A2), ideally customised with the deploy workflow's `job_workflow_ref` (📖 R3.4.5; on Team ⚠️ G10).
- **CI → GCP:** Workload Identity Federation restricted to Papaya's GitHub organization, which Google
  requires (📖 R3.4.5b).
- **k0s, GCP and Firebase for humans:** same principles; mechanisms not researched (G1–G3). Today
  k0s is reached with kubeconfigs, no SSO (GĐ-4, unconfirmed). Interim: no admin kubeconfig and no GCP
  owner role on laptops; prod deploys only from CI. Firebase is not on the GCP BAA list (📖 R5.5.3), so
  Firebase Hosting must hold no PHI (⚠️ R5.7 #7).

**Audit evidence.** Identity Center assignment export (S1), CloudTrail grant events per JIT request, SCP and trust-policy code, Access Analyzer results from phase 2, and a quarterly access review; full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).

**Cost / value.** Engineers lose standing prod write and keep a free non-prod loop. Prod reads stay
fast for metrics and metadata, but shrink during the transition: because the engineer's access is the
agent's access, from phase 1 the engineer too loses raw logs and configuration of services not yet
redacted or moved to runtime secrets. Configuration values come from the IaC code instead (layer 1
above); raw logs that may hold customer data need an L3-data grant. The data owner is not on the
on-call schedule, so at night the grant is approved by the on-call approver alone and the data owner
reviews it the next working day [design]; the wait still counts against S7. This is
the largest cost of the first months. Compliance gets least privilege that is enforced.

## Layer 2 — Agent runtime controls

**Principle.** Agent-side controls are hygiene, not the boundary. They are central, versioned in git
and the same for everyone. Defaults are safe; overrides are measured. The session that reads
untrusted content holds as little power as possible (📖 R6.1.2).

**On Papaya's stack**

- **Delivery:** server-managed settings (available on Team, 📖 R1.1.5) for all laptops. With MDM, also
  an endpoint file; by default one managed source supplies most keys, so the two must carry the same
  keys or use `managedSourcesBehavior: "merge"` (📖 R1.1.3, R1.1.4). MDM is unknown; both are prepared.
- **Baseline** (template: Anthropic's `settings-hipaa.json`, 📖 R5.5.4). All keys 📖 at the row cited. Only the phase-1 subset ([rollout plan](03-rollout-plan.md) item 1.18) ships first; the other keys (sandbox, `allowManagedHooksOnly`, most credential denies, `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly`, `allowedProviders`, `forceLoginOrgUUID`, the `ask` rule for WebFetch, and the other deny rules) arrive in phase 2 (OD4):

  | Key | Value and reason |
  |---|---|
  | `permissions.defaultMode` | `default` (Manual). A default, not a lock: users can switch to auto; VS Code remembers the last pick (D1, R6.9.3). |
  | `permissions.allow` | Two exact repo scripts (`npm test`, `npm run lint`) [design]. Read-only commands need no rule: a built-in set runs without a prompt in every mode (R6.9.3); wildcard rules such as `Bash(git log *)` can write files (examples finding 19). Phase 1 also denies `Read(~/.aws/**)` and sets `autoMode.classifyAllShell` (OD21). |
  | `allowManagedPermissionRulesOnly` | `true`, one rule set (D1, research 6.9.4 Q4; R1.2.5). Cost: project and user rules are ignored, so the managed set must carry every deny/ask rule projects need; prompts likely rise (⚠️ research 6.9.4 Q4). |
  | `permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode` | `"disable"`: removes bypass mode (P3a; R1.2.2). Auto mode, where a classifier approves instead of a person, stays available (D1) and is measured through `permission_mode`. |
  | `permissions.deny` / `ask` | Deny credential paths (R5.5.4; `Read(...)` syntax ⚠️ R1.8 #5). Ask for `WebFetch`, which the sandbox domain list does not limit (R1.6.2); cost: a prompt per fetch. The HIPAA template denies WebFetch (R5.5.4); "ask" is a deliberate deviation so that documentation lookups still work. Ask for `Bash(aws *)`, `Bash(pulumi *)`, `Bash(serverless *)`, which prompts even in auto mode (📖 [auto mode config](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/auto-mode-config.md); examples finding 22). Credential denies extend to the known credential stores of Papaya's stack; some paths are ⚠️ and some stores are not covered (examples E8, with every deviation from the template). |
  | `requiredMinimumVersion` | ≥ 2.1.310 in phase 2: 2.1.285 for `allowedProviders` (R1.1.15), 2.1.310 so `allowManagedHooksOnly` also blocks monitors of plugins that are not force-enabled (📖 [settings reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#allowmanagedhooksonly)); which also covers `--restricted` (2.1.248, R6.9.1b) and the plugin-pin fix (2.1.179, R6.2.7); ≥ 2.1.295 if any managed hook uses `onFailure: "block"` (R1.5.2); and ≥ the latest fixed advisory at rollout (R6.3.9). It does not end running sessions and fails open on a bad value (R1.1.13). |
  | `allowedProviders` + `forceLoginOrgUUID` | `["anthropic"]` + Papaya's org; closes most bypasses on **endpoint-managed** machines (R1.1.15). `forceLoginOrgUUID` checks claude.ai sign-ins only, not Claude Console sign-ins (R5.5.5); with it set, sessions on `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` or `apiKeyHelper` are refused (R1.11.3.11). |
  | `allowManagedHooksOnly` | `true` (R1.5.4). |
  | `autoMode` | `classifyAllShell: true` and the template's `"$defaults"` pins, which keep the built-in rules; not a boundary (examples finding 25). |
  | sandbox | `sandbox.enabled`, `failIfUnavailable`, `allowUnsandboxedCommands: false`, narrow `network.allowedDomains` locked by `network.allowManagedDomainsOnly`; `credentials` / `filesystem.denyRead` on `~/.aws` and the other credential stores, which the sandbox can otherwise read (R1.6.3, R1.6.4). Reads are a denylist and allowed domains are exfiltration paths; `git push`, `gh`, Docker and private-registry `npm ci` fail inside the sandbox (limits and costs: examples E8). |
  | `sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed` | Left at its default `true` (owner decision OD12). This widens D1's "Manual + allowlist": every sandboxed command, writes in the working directory and calls to allowed domains included, runs without a prompt. Detail: sandboxed Bash runs without a prompt, so in Manual mode prompts are for edits, unsandboxed commands and fetches, not every command (R5.5.5b). A deliberate choice: the sandbox (no `~/.aws`, allowlisted network) is the control for those commands. The HIPAA README says to set `false` if policy needs a person to approve each command (R5.5.5b); cost of `false`: a prompt per command. |
  | MCP, plugins | Layer 4. |
  | OTel | Exporter on, content flags `0` (R1.1.20, R5.5.4). |

- **Trade-off on AWS credentials [design].** With `~/.aws` hidden from the sandbox, phase 2 lists
  `aws *`, `pulumi *` and `serverless *` in `sandbox.excludedCommands`. Excluded commands run "with
  full access" (📖 R1.6.4), network included ("no filesystem restrictions and no network proxy", 📖 [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#run-commands-outside-the-sandbox-with-excludedcommands)). Matching follows `Bash(...)` rule
  syntax on the command text (same page; details in examples finding 22); each excluded
  call prompts through the `ask` rules above. This is worse than an
  egress channel: `pulumi preview` runs the Pulumi program and `serverless` loads its config and
  plugins, all code in the repo that the agent can edit, so excluding them lets repo code run
  outside the sandbox with network access and with `~/.aws` readable (⚠️ inference). For these
  commands the sandbox gives no protection. And an injected `aws` command could send out the SSO
  token cache itself. That token likely opens every role assigned to the engineer for the rest of the
  portal session (📖 R2.1.5; token reuse ⚠️ R2.2.2), probably including JIT or data-read grants added
  later in that session (⚠️ inference). Mitigations [design]: a short portal session (📖 R2.1.5); end
  the existing portal session and sign in fresh **before** a JIT or data-read grant is created
  (whether ending a session invalidates a token already stolen is unverified ⚠️; ending it does not
  end role sessions, 📖 R2.4.3); an SCP that denies writes to resources outside Papaya's organization using
  `aws:ResourceOrgID` (key 📖 R2.3.8), on every OU, since the token can be stolen from a non-prod
  session; legitimate writes to outside resources need exceptions (⚠️ not inventoried). That SCP only stops Papaya's own credentials writing to a
  foreign bucket; it does not stop a command that sends the token to a non-AWS endpoint or uses the
  attacker's credentials (⚠️ inference). Prefer running `pulumi` and `serverless` against real
  accounts only in CI; on laptops keep them to non-prod roles, and move them into the phase-3
  container. Residual risk: token theft during a session. It is accepted
  because the engineer holds no **standing** prod write and no **standing** PHI read; during a JIT
  or data-read window the protection is the process rule in layer 1 (D2). Stronger option, phase 3:
  a separate OS user or container for prod-reading sessions
  (⚠️ R6.5 #2).
- **Session types:**

  | Session | Identity | Flags | Enforcement |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Daily development (laptop) | non-prod roles + `ProdReadMetadata` | baseline | Auto mode by choice (D1); `--restricted` recommended (D3). |
  | Incident analysis (laptop) | meant to be `ProdReadMetadata` only | `--restricted --tools "Bash,Read,Grep,Glob"`, started in an empty scratch directory, not the repo [design] | Process rule (D3, research 6.9.4 Q1–Q2). No WebFetch, and file tools confined to the working directory (📖 R6.9.1b); Edit/Write are excluded only if `--tools` acts as an exclusive list (⚠️ unverified), but Bash can still write in its working directory (📖 R1.6.3) and call any role in the cache. |
  | CI agent (hosted runner) | own GitHub App token; never `production` | `--restricted`, explicit `--tools`; all rules in a managed-settings file on the runner | Workflow file under CODEOWNERS (D3, research 6.9.4 Q5). The file is advisory if `Bash` is in `--tools` (layer 5). |
  | JIT terminal | JIT grant | no agent | Process rule (D2). |
  | Auto-mode environment (phase 3) | non-prod only | auto encouraged | D1 option (c). |

- **Phase-1 interim posture:** the sandbox and most credential denies arrive in phase 2 (OD4), so for
  the first 30–60 days the network is open to every Bash command, and `~/.aws` is protected only by
  the `Read(~/.aws/**)` deny rule (OD21), which does not cover a command that reads files without
  naming them or a script that opens them itself (📖 [permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md)); in auto mode the classifier
  is the only other gate. Impact is bounded once standing prod write is removed at the
  end of phase 1 (layer 1); before that, today's exposure continues, and token theft is easier in this window.
- **Hard limits:** Bash rules are not a boundary (📖 R1.2.6); hooks fail open unless
  `"onFailure": "block"` (📖 R1.5.2); `--restricted` cannot be forced by a setting (📖 R6.9.1), and a `PATH` wrapper on laptops can be bypassed (⚠️ R6.9.1c);
  on laptops **without MDM**, a different login, an API key or a `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_*` variable skips
  server-managed settings, `allowedProviders` included (📖 R1.1.7; ⚠️ R1.8 #3, G11). So S5's
  "nobody can turn off all prompts unnoticed" is likely unreachable without MDM (⚠️).
- **Auto memory:** engineers review it and delete it after a suspicious session; residual risk with a
  named owner (D3).
- **Fallback:** switch to `disableAutoMode` (📖 R1.2.2) if the planted-injection test steers auto mode, a serious
  advisory appears, or an audit finds auto mode touched a protected scope (D1).

**Audit evidence.** Managed settings as an expected copy in git with PR approvals, a monthly diff with the console export (G18), sampled `/status`, and OTel permission-mode metrics; full register: [04-compliance-mapping.md](04-compliance-mapping.md#register).

**Cost / value.** More prompts than auto mode, partly offset by the built-in read-only commands and
the two allowed repo scripts. Compliance
gets one organization policy with evidence instead of personal choices (P3c).
