# ADR-0011: Database schema changes and data fixes go through the pipeline like any prod change

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission, after the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; OD29)
- **Scope:** Aurora PostgreSQL schema migrations, GraphQL-engine (Hasura) metadata, and data fixes on prod

## 1. Context

"Every prod change is a pull request" (ADR-0001) had no designed path for the two most frequent
prod changes of a claims platform on Aurora with a GraphQL engine: schema migrations and data fixes
(a stuck claim, a payout to retry). Once standing prod write is removed (rollout 1.16), nobody has a
legitimate way to run them, which invites a shared database account or an admin endpoint: the
shortcut the framework exists to remove. Data fixes also touch one tenant's customer data, which
layer 6 treats as L3-data. IAM database authentication is not logged by CloudTrail (📖 R9.2.11).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. JIT grant with `psql` for data fixes; migrations at app start | Fast; no new tooling | An approved command list, not an approved change (ADR-0005's weakness) for routine work; migrations run with the app's role |
| B. Migration and data-fix files in the monorepo, applied by the deploy workflow with a database role of its own, behind the risk stop | Same gate, same evidence as every other change | A migration job and two wrapper scripts per migration tool; data fixes need two approvers |
| C. A separate database change tool with its own approvals | Purpose-built | A second approval system outside GitHub; a side path (T20) |

## 3. Decision

Option B [design]:

- **Files:** migrations, GraphQL-engine metadata and data fixes live under `db/<service>/`; data
  fixes under `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`, one tenant per file, with an
  `-- expected_rows: N` header.
- **Approval:** migrations and metadata as any deployable path (domain owner, on-call in an
  incident). Data fixes are **L3-data-write**: a code owner plus a different person from that
  tenant's data-owner team, checked by the approval-gate app (E12, rule R4); in an incident the
  on-call approver stands in and the data owner reviews the next working day (layer 6).
- **Apply:** a `sql` job of the deploy workflow lists the pending files, runs the risk stop on them
  (`--tool sql`: DROP, TRUNCATE, column type changes, unscoped DELETE/UPDATE, grants, roles,
  row-level security, COPY, function bodies and every metadata change stop for a stack owner's
  approval), then applies exactly the classified files, each in its own transaction; a data fix
  whose affected-row count differs from its header is rolled back.
- **Credentials:** the job's OIDC role may only `rds-db:connect` as the migration database user
  (📖 R9.2.11); no person holds database credentials.
- **Evidence:** the PR, the job log and summary (statement kinds and row counts, never values),
  the risk-stop record; database-side activity through Database Activity Streams (layer 7),
  because IAM database authentication is not in CloudTrail.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the most common prod changes get the same gate and evidence chain as code; data
  fixes are scoped to one tenant and approved by its data owner; no standing database access.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** a data fix takes a PR, two approvals and a deploy run instead of a
  `psql` session; the two `tools/db/` scripts must be written for Papaya's migration tool
  (unknown here); the SQL classifier is a heuristic, not a parser (examples E7).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** a destructive statement hidden in a form the heuristic does not
  know (function bodies and `EXECUTE` already stop); a wrong `expected_rows` is caught only if the
  count differs; long migrations hold locks (expand/contract recommended, not enforced).
- **Next steps:** `tools/db/` wrappers and the migration role in phase 1, before standing prod write
  is removed (rollout 1.23).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Database changes"), layer 6 (L3-data), layer 7 (Database Activity Streams).
- Examples E3 (`sql` job), E7 (SQL rules), E12 (rule R4).
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004, ADR-0009, ADR-0012.

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='docs/01-framework.md'
s=open(p).read()
def rep(o,n):
    global s
    assert s.count(o)==1,o[:80]
    s=s.replace(o,n)
rep("""Until a service's logs are redacted at source
    (layer 6), it gets that service's metrics only.""","""Until a service's logs are redacted at source
    and masked (layer 6, OD28), it gets that service's metrics only.""")
rep("""| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |""",
"""| **L3-data** | Real customer data read | one tenant's failed claim record | an approver ≠ requester and an agreement (GĐ-9); data-owner co-approval [design], beyond GĐ-9; at night, see layer 6 | layer 6 |
| **L3-data-write** | Data fix on one tenant's records | retry a stuck payout | a code owner plus a different member of that tenant's data-owner team, checked by the approval-gate app; in an incident the on-call approver stands in and the data owner reviews next working day (OD29) | PR → `sql` deploy job ("Database changes" below) |""")
rep("""- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if""","""- **Database changes (OD29, ADR-0011) [design].** Aurora schema migrations, GraphQL-engine
  (Hasura) metadata and data fixes are files under `db/<service>/`, merged like code and applied by
  a `sql` job of the deploy workflow (examples E3):
  - the job assumes a role that may only `rds-db:connect` as the migration database user
    (IAM database authentication, 📖 R9.2.11); no person holds database credentials;
  - it lists the pending files through `tools/db/` wrappers around Papaya's migration tool (an L3
    path; the tool is not known here), runs the risk stop on them with `--tool sql`, and applies
    exactly the classified files, each in its own transaction;
  - the SQL risk stop (a heuristic, not a parser; examples E7) stops on DROP, TRUNCATE, column type
    changes, DELETE or UPDATE without a top-level WHERE, grants, roles, row-level security, COPY,
    function bodies and `EXECUTE`; every metadata change stops too, because it holds row
    permissions per role, i.e. tenant isolation;
  - data fixes (`db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`) touch one tenant, declare
    `-- expected_rows: N`, and are rolled back when the count differs; approval is L3-data-write
    (table above); the job summary shows statement kinds and row counts, never values;
  - IAM database authentication is not in CloudTrail (📖 R9.2.11), so database-side evidence comes
    from Database Activity Streams (layer 7). Expand/contract migrations are recommended, not
    enforced. Cost: a data fix takes a PR and two approvals instead of a `psql` session.
- **Merge approval = deploy approval** only if""")
rep("""  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].""",
"""  - logs redacted at source with raw payloads in a separate log group; alerts carry IDs, not payloads [design].
    Redaction lives in application code, so one approved PR that logs a whole event would put
    PHI in a log group the agent reads. A second layer outside the code (OD28) [design]:
    - a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy on every log group `ProdReadMetadata` reads, set
      **before** the group is opened, because masking applies at ingestion only; masked data is
      hidden "at all egress points, including CloudWatch Logs Insights" (📖 R9.2.7);
    - custom identifiers keyed on field names (national ID, HKID, bank account, diagnosis,
      insured name; examples E14), because AWS has no managed identifier for Vietnam, Thailand
      or Hong Kong (📖 R9.2.8); at most 10, each regex ≤ 200 characters (📖 R9.2.9);
    - no agent-usable role holds `logs:Unmask`, and none gets `CloudWatchLogsFullAccess`, which
      includes it (📖 R9.2.7; E6 test);
    - a required SAST rule against logging whole events or payload objects in the claims
      services' handlers (S10; product open, G4); a log-level change already stops at the risk
      stop (`logging` property), because debug output can carry PHI.
    Limit: field-name masking catches structured logs, not free text in a message. It is a second
    layer; code review and the SAST rule remain the first. Cost: $0.12 per GB scanned
    (📖 R9.2.10) and masked values while debugging.""")
rep("""  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days, so exported (📖 R3.5.6);""","""  - **evidence bucket** (OD30) [design]: an S3 bucket in the log-archive account with Object Lock
    in compliance mode, 6 years, which nobody, root included, can shorten or delete (📖 R9.2.12;
    a new bucket, since enabling it on an existing one was not confirmed). From phase 1 a nightly
    workflow writes the last day's merged PRs with their reviews and check runs, and the logs and
    artifacts (`risk-summary`) of deploy runs, through a role that may only `PutObject`
    (examples E13). Actions keeps logs 90 days by default, at most 400 (📖 R9.1.8): set 400 as
    a buffer;
  - GitHub org audit log kept 180 days (📖 R3.5.6). Its REST API is documented for Enterprise
    Cloud, not Team (📖 R9.1.5), so an org owner exports it monthly from the UI (JSON) into the
    evidence bucket, a manual step in the monthly report (📖 R9.1.7);
  - **JIT and real-data request records** (OD30): an issue in a dedicated Linear team, from a
    template with required fields (command list or store, scope, tenant, reason, incident link,
    agreement); the approver approves by moving it to an "Approved" state. Linear's audit log is
    Enterprise-only and kept 90 days, and its CSV export has no field history (📖 R9.1.14), so a
    webhook receiver in the tooling account (the approval-gate app's) writes every change, with
    the previous values Linear sends, to the evidence bucket. Not Slack;""")
rep("""| OD27 |""","""| OD28 | PHI could reach the agent through a log group it may read, if one approved PR logs a whole event (review A-1b) | CloudWatch Logs masking with custom identifiers on those log groups, set before they open; no `logs:Unmask` for agent-usable roles; a SAST rule against logging whole events. Stated as a second layer: AWS has no managed identifiers for VN/TH/HK. |
| OD29 | No designed path for schema migrations and data fixes (review E-1) | `sql` job of the deploy workflow with its own database role (IAM auth), SQL risk stop, metadata changes always stop, data fixes per tenant with expected rows and a data owner's approval (L3-data-write); ADR-0011. A hard prerequisite of removing standing prod write. |
| OD30 | Evidence before phase 2 can expire; JIT and data-read approvals have no store (review C-2, C-3) | From phase 1: evidence bucket with Object Lock (compliance, 6 years), nightly export of PRs, reviews, checks, deploy logs and artifacts; monthly manual export of the org audit log; Linear template for JIT and data-read requests, mirrored to the bucket by webhook. Closes O-1 and O-4. |
| OD27 |""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
print('ok')
EOF

- **What you do:** with `ProdReadMetadata` (1-hour session) you and your agent read metrics, metadata
  and logs that are redacted at source. Lambda configuration is readable per service once its secrets
  are resolved at runtime; until then, read timeout and memory from the IaC code.
- **Approval:** none (L0).
- **Cost to know:** in the first months, raw logs of services not yet redacted are not readable
  without a data-read request (section 5). This is the largest cost of the transition.
- **Only if the PR path cannot be used** (GitHub Actions down, broken pipeline, an operation not in
  IaC): end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then request a JIT grant in the incident
  channel outside GitHub, with the exact commands. The on-call approver approves before the grant.
  You get `InfraOperator-<service>` (1-hour role session; the real window can approach 2 h) and type
  the commands yourself, in a terminal **without an agent**. Afterwards your commands are compared
  with CloudTrail (by hand in phase 1, by a job from phase 2), and you open a PR that codifies the change.
- **What you do:** end your AWS portal session and sign in fresh, then request it with one tenant,
  purpose, store, time window and the agreement that covers it. You get a data-read role for 1 hour.
  After reading one tenant's data, do not post to shared places without review.

A model provider that processes the prompt in clear text, and may keep it or review it for abuse, is a recipient, not a passive pipe. # ADR-0011: Database schema changes and data fixes go through the pipeline like any prod change

- **Status:** Accepted
- **Date:** 2026-11-09
- **Decided by:** owner of this submission, after the independent review (`work/07-review.md`; OD29)
- **Scope:** Aurora PostgreSQL schema migrations, GraphQL-engine (Hasura) metadata, and data fixes on prod

## 1. Context

"Every prod change is a pull request" (ADR-0001) had no designed path for the two most frequent
prod changes of a claims platform on Aurora with a GraphQL engine: schema migrations and data fixes
(a stuck claim, a payout to retry). Once standing prod write is removed (rollout 1.16), nobody has a
legitimate way to run them, which invites a shared database account or an admin endpoint: the
shortcut the framework exists to remove. Data fixes also touch one tenant's customer data, which
layer 6 treats as L3-data. IAM database authentication is not logged by CloudTrail (📖 R9.2.11).

## 2. Options considered

| Option | Pros | Cons |
|---|---|---|
| A. JIT grant with `psql` for data fixes; migrations at app start | Fast; no new tooling | An approved command list, not an approved change (ADR-0005's weakness) for routine work; migrations run with the app's role |
| B. Migration and data-fix files in the monorepo, applied by the deploy workflow with a database role of its own, behind the risk stop | Same gate, same evidence as every other change | A migration job and two wrapper scripts per migration tool; data fixes need two approvers |
| C. A separate database change tool with its own approvals | Purpose-built | A second approval system outside GitHub; a side path (T20) |

## 3. Decision

Option B [design]:

- **Files:** migrations, GraphQL-engine metadata and data fixes live under `db/<service>/`; data
  fixes under `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`, one tenant per file, with an
  `-- expected_rows: N` header.
- **Approval:** migrations and metadata as any deployable path (domain owner, on-call in an
  incident). Data fixes are **L3-data-write**: a code owner plus a different person from that
  tenant's data-owner team, checked by the approval-gate app (E12, rule R4); in an incident the
  on-call approver stands in and the data owner reviews the next working day (layer 6).
- **Apply:** a `sql` job of the deploy workflow lists the pending files, runs the risk stop on them
  (`--tool sql`: DROP, TRUNCATE, column type changes, unscoped DELETE/UPDATE, grants, roles,
  row-level security, COPY, function bodies and every metadata change stop for a stack owner's
  approval), then applies exactly the classified files, each in its own transaction; a data fix
  whose affected-row count differs from its header is rolled back.
- **Credentials:** the job's OIDC role may only `rds-db:connect` as the migration database user
  (📖 R9.2.11); no person holds database credentials.
- **Evidence:** the PR, the job log and summary (statement kinds and row counts, never values),
  the risk-stop record; database-side activity through Database Activity Streams (layer 7),
  because IAM database authentication is not in CloudTrail.

## 4. Consequences

- **Positive:** the most common prod changes get the same gate and evidence chain as code; data
  fixes are scoped to one tenant and approved by its data owner; no standing database access.
- **Negative / trade-offs:** a data fix takes a PR, two approvals and a deploy run instead of a
  `psql` session; the two `tools/db/` scripts must be written for Papaya's migration tool
  (unknown here); the SQL classifier is a heuristic, not a parser (examples E7).
- **Risks & how we watch them:** a destructive statement hidden in a form the heuristic does not
  know (function bodies and `EXECUTE` already stop); a wrong `expected_rows` is caught only if the
  count differs; long migrations hold locks (expand/contract recommended, not enforced).
- **Next steps:** `tools/db/` wrappers and the migration role in phase 1, before standing prod write
  is removed (rollout 1.23).

## 5. References

- Framework layer 3 ("Database changes"), layer 6 (L3-data), layer 7 (Database Activity Streams).
- Examples E3 (`sql` job), E7 (SQL rules), E12 (rule R4).
- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004, ADR-0009, ADR-0012.

29	- **Files:** migrations, GraphQL-engine metadata and data fixes live under `db/<service>/`; data
30	  fixes under `db/<service>/data-fixes/<tenant>/<ticket>.sql`, one tenant per file, with an
31	  `-- expected_rows: N` header.
32	- **Approval:** migrations and metadata as any deployable path (domain owner, on-call in an
33	  incident). Data fixes are **L3-data-write**: a code owner plus a different person from that
34	  tenant's data-owner team, checked by the approval-gate app (E12, rule R4); in an incident the
35	  on-call approver stands in and the data owner reviews the next working day (layer 6).
36	- **Apply:** a `sql` job of the deploy workflow lists the pending files, runs the risk stop on them
37	  (`--tool sql`: DROP, TRUNCATE, column type changes, unscoped DELETE/UPDATE, grants, roles,
38	  row-level security, COPY, function bodies and every metadata change stop for a stack owner's
39	  approval), then applies exactly the classified files, each in its own transaction; a data fix
40	  whose affected-row count differs from its header is rolled back.
41	- **Credentials:** the job's OIDC role may only `rds-db:connect` as the migration database user
42	  (📖 R9.2.11); no person holds database credentials.
43	- **Evidence:** the PR, the job log and summary (statement kinds and row counts, never values),
44	  the risk-stop record; database-side activity through Database Activity Streams (layer 7),
45	  because IAM database authentication is not in CloudTrail.
46	
47	## 4. Consequences
48	
49	- **Positive:** the most common prod changes get the same gate and evidence chain as code; data
50	  fixes are scoped to one tenant and approved by its data owner; no standing database access.
51	- **Negative / trade-offs:** a data fix takes a PR, two approvals and a deploy run instead of a
52	  `psql` session; the two `tools/db/` scripts must be written for Papaya's migration tool
53	  (unknown here); the SQL classifier is a heuristic, not a parser (examples E7).
54	- **Risks & how we watch them:** a destructive statement hidden in a form the heuristic does not
55	  know (function bodies and `EXECUTE` already stop); a wrong `expected_rows` is caught only if the
56	  count differs; long migrations hold locks (expand/contract recommended, not enforced).
57	- **Next steps:** `tools/db/` wrappers and the migration role in phase 1, before standing prod write
58	  is removed (rollout 1.23).
59	
60	## 5. References
61	
62	- Framework layer 3 ("Database changes"), layer 6 (L3-data), layer 7 (Database Activity Streams).
63	- Examples E3 (`sql` job), E7 (SQL rules), E12 (rule R4).
64	- Related: ADR-0001, ADR-0004, ADR-0009, ADR-0012.

"""Adapters from each tool's preview JSON to the normalized format used by classify.py.

⚠️ NOT VERIFIED. Neither tool's JSON structure is documented in the research for this
submission (work/02-research.md R4.1.1 and R4.4.2 only name the `--json` flag), and neither
tool was run here. The field names below are assumptions to check against real output
before use. Any input they cannot read raises an error, and classify.py then stops the
deploy (fail closed).

Assumed shapes:
  pulumi preview --json:
    {"steps": [{"op": "update", "urn": "urn:pulumi:<stack>::<project>::<type>::<name>",
                "newState": {"type": "...", "inputs": {...}},
                "oldState": {"type": "...", "inputs": {...}}}]}
    Pulumi ops seen in its docs/CLI output: same, create, update, delete, replace,
    create-replacement, delete-replaced, read, refresh, import ... (⚠️ list not checked).
  serverless diff --json (sf-core >= 4.37.0):
    {"resources": [{"logicalId": "...", "type": "AWS::...", "action": "add|modify|remove",
                    "replacement": true|false, "properties": {<changed properties only>}}]}
"""
import hashlib
import json
import re

PULUMI_OPS = {
    "same": "same",
    "create": "create",
    "update": "update",
    "delete": "delete",
    "replace": "replace",
    "create-replacement": "replace",
    "delete-replaced": "replace",
    "read": "same",
}


def _digest(*values):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(values, sort_keys=True, default=str).encode()).hexdigest()


def _changed_keys(old, new):
    return sorted(k for k in set(old) | set(new) if old.get(k) != new.get(k))


def pulumi(raw):
    changes = []
    for step in raw["steps"]:
        urn = step["urn"]
        name = urn.rsplit("::", 1)[-1]
        state = step.get("newState") or step.get("oldState") or {}
        # URN type part is "parent$...$type" for child resources; keep the last segment.
        rtype = state.get("type") or urn.split("::")[-2].rsplit("$", 1)[-1]
        old = (step.get("oldState") or {}).get("inputs") or {}
        new = (step.get("newState") or {}).get("inputs") or {}
        changes.append({
            "type": rtype,
            "name": name,
            "op": PULUMI_OPS.get(step["op"], step["op"]),  # unknown ops pass through -> risky
            "changed_keys": _changed_keys(old, new),
            "detail_digest": _digest(old, new),
        })
    return {"changes": changes}


SLS_ACTIONS = {"add": "create", "modify": "update", "remove": "delete"}


def serverless(raw):
    changes = []
    for r in raw["resources"]:
        op = SLS_ACTIONS.get(r["action"], r["action"])
        if op == "update" and r.get("replacement"):
            op = "replace"
        props = dict(r.get("properties") or {})
        # ⚠️ Values that change on every `serverless package` would make the hash unstable, so
        # an approval could never match. From memory, not checked: the Lambda code location
        # (Code.S3Key) holds a timestamped artifact path, and AWS::Lambda::Version logical IDs
        # carry a code hash. `Code` is left out of the hash and of changed_keys (it is code, not
        # access); Version changes are left out of the hash only. Not handled: resources that
        # reference the version logical ID (aliases, provisioned concurrency) also change on
        # every build, so their stacks may never get a stable hash.
        if r["type"] == "AWS::Lambda::Function":
            props.pop("Code", None)
        changes.append({
            "type": r["type"],
            "name": r["logicalId"],
            "op": op,
            "changed_keys": sorted(props),
            "detail_digest": _digest(props),
            "volatile": r["type"] == "AWS::Lambda::Version",
        })
    return {"changes": changes}


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- SQL (framework layer 3,
# "Database changes"; ADR-0011) [design]. Not a SQL parser: a heuristic that sorts each
# statement of a pending migration or data-fix file into a kind. classify.py decides which
# kinds are risky; anything it cannot read safely (function bodies, DO blocks, EXECUTE) gets
# the kind `dynamic_sql`, which stops the deploy (fail closed).
#
# Input, written by the deploy step that lists pending files (how it finds them depends on
# Papaya's migration tool, not known here):
#   {"files": [{"path": "db/migrations/20261109_add_col.sql", "kind": "migration",
#               "sql": "<file content>"}]}
#   kind: migration | data-fix | metadata
#   `metadata` = a GraphQL-engine metadata file (Hasura: permissions per role, i.e. access and
#   tenant isolation). It is not parsed: every change gets the kind `metadata`, which stops.

_SQL_KINDS = [
    # (kind, pattern on one statement after comments, strings and nested parentheses are gone)
    ("privilege", r"^(GRANT|REVOKE)\b|^(CREATE|ALTER|DROP)\s+(ROLE|USER|GROUP|POLICY)\b"
                  r"|^ALTER\s+DEFAULT\s+PRIVILEGES\b|\bSECURITY\s+DEFINER\b|\bOWNER\s+TO\b"),
    ("row_security", r"^ALTER\s+TABLE\b.*\b(ENABLE|DISABLE|FORCE|NO\s+FORCE)\s+ROW\s+LEVEL\s+SECURITY\b"),
    ("truncate", r"^TRUNCATE\b"),
    ("drop_column", r"^ALTER\s+TABLE\b.*\bDROP\s+(COLUMN\b|CONSTRAINT\b|(IF\s+EXISTS\s+)?\w)"),
    ("alter_column_type", r"^ALTER\s+TABLE\b.*\bALTER\s+(COLUMN\s+)?\S+\s+(SET\s+DATA\s+)?TYPE\b"),
    ("drop", r"^DROP\b"),
    ("copy", r"^COPY\b"),
    ("dynamic_sql", r"^(DO|EXECUTE)\b|^CALL\b"),
    ("delete", r"^(WITH\b.*?)?\bDELETE\s+FROM\b"),
    ("update", r"^(WITH\b.*?)?\bUPDATE\s+\S+\s+(AS\s+\S+\s+)?SET\b"),
    ("insert", r"^(WITH\b.*?)?\bINSERT\s+INTO\b"),
    ("alter", r"^ALTER\b"),
    ("create", r"^CREATE\b"),
]


def _sql_statements(text):
    """Split SQL into upper-case statements without comments, string literals or bodies.

    Returns (statements, has_body): has_body is True if a dollar-quoted body ($$ or $tag$)
    was found; its content cannot be classified."""
    has_body = bool(re.search(r"\$\w*\$", text))
    text = re.sub(r"\$(\w*)\$.*?\$\1\$", " $BODY$ ", text, flags=re.S)  # function / DO bodies
    text = re.sub(r"/\*.*?\*/", " ", text, flags=re.S)                  # block comments
    text = re.sub(r"--[^\n]*", " ", text)                               # line comments
    text = re.sub(r"'(?:[^']|'')*'", "''", text)                        # string literals
    text = re.sub(r'"(?:[^"]|"")*"', "ident", text)                     # quoted identifiers
    out = []
    for stmt in text.split(";"):
        s = " ".join(stmt.split()).upper()
        if s:
            out.append(s)
    return out, has_body


def _top_level(stmt):
    """Remove everything inside parentheses, so a WHERE in a subquery is not mistaken for the
    statement's own WHERE."""
    prev = None
    while prev != stmt:
        prev, stmt = stmt, re.sub(r"\([^()]*\)", "()", stmt)
    return stmt


def sql_kinds(text):
    """Sorted kinds found in one SQL file, e.g. ["create", "delete_unscoped"]."""
    statements, has_body = _sql_statements(text)
    kinds = set()
    if has_body:
        kinds.add("dynamic_sql")
    for s in statements:
        top = _top_level(s)
        for kind, pattern in _SQL_KINDS:
            if re.search(pattern, top):
                if kind in ("delete", "update"):
                    # Scoped only if the statement itself (not a subquery) has a WHERE.
                    verb = "DELETE" if kind == "delete" else "UPDATE"
                    tail = top[top.find(verb):]
                    kind += "_scoped" if re.search(r"\bWHERE\b", tail) else "_unscoped"
                kinds.add(kind)
                break
        else:
            kinds.add("other")
    return sorted(kinds)


def sql(raw):
    changes = []
    for f in raw["files"]:
        if f["kind"] not in ("migration", "data-fix", "metadata"):
            raise ValueError(f"unknown SQL file kind '{f['kind']}'")
        kinds = ["metadata"] if f["kind"] == "metadata" else sql_kinds(f["sql"])
        changes.append({
            "type": f"sql:{f['kind']}",
            "name": f["path"],
            "op": "update",
            "changed_keys": kinds,  # statement kinds only, never SQL text
            "detail_digest": _digest(f["path"], f["sql"]),  # the approval covers this exact SQL
        })
    return {"changes": changes}


def normalized(raw):
    for c in raw["changes"]:
        for key in ("type", "name", "op"):
            if not isinstance(c.get(key), str):
                raise ValueError(f"change without '{key}'")
    return raw


ADAPTERS = {"pulumi": pulumi, "serverless": serverless, "sql": sql, "normalized": normalized}

# Caller: every push to main (= every merged, approved PR) deploys through the reusable
# deploy-prod.yml. Framework layer 3: the merge to main is the approval gate (ADR-0003).
# No workflow_dispatch: a manual run could pick another ref; `production` only allows `main`
# anyway (environment-production/), but the fewer triggers the smaller the attack surface.
name: deploy-on-main

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  claims-data:
    uses: $/.github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read   # passed to deploy-prod.yml: check out
      id-token: write  # passed to deploy-prod.yml: OIDC to the prod deploy role
    with:
      stack: claims-data
      tool: pulumi
      workdir: infra/pulumi/claims-data

  # The IAM stack: deploy-prod.yml maps stack `iam` to the `production-iam` environment (OD22).
  iam:
    uses: $/.github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read   # passed to deploy-prod.yml: check out
      id-token: write  # passed to deploy-prod.yml: OIDC to the IAM stack's deploy role
    with:
      stack: iam
      tool: pulumi
      workdir: infra/pulumi/iam

  # Database changes of the claims service: migrations and data fixes (ADR-0011, OD29).
  claims-db:
    uses: $/.github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read   # passed to deploy-prod.yml: check out
      id-token: write  # passed to deploy-prod.yml: OIDC to the database change role
    with:
      stack: claims-db
      tool: sql
      workdir: db/claims

  claims-api:
    uses: $/.github/workflows/deploy-prod.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read   # passed to deploy-prod.yml: check out
      id-token: write  # passed to deploy-prod.yml: OIDC to the prod deploy role
    with:
      stack: claims-api
      tool: serverless
      workdir: services/claims

## Quy chuẩn kỹ thuật & Viết code (DevOps Standards)

### 1. Nguyên tắc an toàn & Thực thi (Safety Guardrails)
- **Kiểm soát lệnh phá hủy:** Tuyệt đối không tự ý chạy các lệnh phá hủy như `terraform destroy`, `rm -rf`, xoá namespace Kubernetes, xoá PVC, hoặc `helm uninstall` nếu chưa có sự xác nhận rõ ràng từ người dùng.
- **Thực thi có kiểm soát:** Luôn ưu tiên chạy lệnh preview/diff trước (`terraform plan`, `ansible-playbook --check`, `kubectl diff`, `helm template`) trước khi áp dụng thay đổi.
- **Quản lý Secrets:** Không bao giờ hardcode credentials, private key, token, API key vào code. Luôn dùng biến môi trường, SOPS, HashiCorp Vault, hoặc Ansible Vault.

# DevOps AI Kit — Core rules

You help a DevOps/Cloud engineer who works on real infrastructure (Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Azure/AWS/GCP, on-prem). A mistake here can break running systems and real data. Safety and proof are more important than speed.

## 1. Check the target first

- Before the first command that touches infrastructure in a task, check the target and tell the user: kube context + namespace, terraform workspace/backend, Azure subscription / AWS account / GCP project. If the project's CLAUDE.md has an "Environment registry" table, compare with it.
- Do not change the context, subscription, workspace or kubeconfig yourself. If a change is needed, ask first.
- A context that ends with `-ro` is read-only (the kubeconfig made for the AI). A `Forbidden` error on that context is expected. Do not try to get more permissions. Give the command to the user to run, or prepare a GitOps PR.

## 2. Read-only first, mutating later

- Read-only: get, describe, logs, top, diff, plan, validate, template, lint, `--check`, `--dry-run`, show/list.
- Mutating: apply, create, delete, patch, replace, scale, rollout restart/undo, exec, install/upgrade/rollback/uninstall, terraform apply/import/state, ansible-playbook without `--check`, `git push` to a GitOps repo, SQL DDL/DML, cloud CLI commands that create/update/delete/set.
- Always run a preview before you apply (`terraform plan`, `kubectl diff`, `helm diff`/`helm template`, `ansible-playbook --check --diff`). Give the user a short summary of the preview.
- Right before each mutating command, write 4 lines:
  - **What:** …
  - **Target:** the exact context / namespace / resource
  - **Reversible?:** yes / no / partly, and why
  - **Undo:** the exact command, or "not possible, needs backup X"
- Do not add `-auto-approve`, `--yes`, `--force`, `--grace-period=0` unless the user clearly asks for it.

## 3. Risk levels

| Level | Example | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| L0 read-only | debug, read logs, write docs | do it directly |
| L1 dev/sandbox, can be undone | test a component on a dev cluster | short plan → do → verify → change record |
| L2 shared environment, stateless | upgrade Grafana on prod | ask the user to run `/infra-task` |
| L3 stateful / cannot be undone / network / IAM | migrate a DB, change StorageClass, change CIDR, IAM | stop and ask for `/infra-task`; a backup that was test-restored is required |

If you are not sure about the level, choose the higher one and explain why.

## 4. Existing systems (brownfield)

- Follow the conventions that already exist in the repo/cluster, even if they are different from the kit's standards. Write the differences in the **Recommendations** part of your report. Do not fix things outside the task.
- Do not do extra cleanup (rename, refactor, version upgrade) outside the agreed scope.
- **Do not trust one source.** In a running system the code, the last apply and the live state can differ, and ignore rules hide some differences from the tools (Terraform `ignore_changes`, Argo CD `ignoreDifferences`, an HPA that owns `replicas`, apps without selfHeal, manual `kubectl edit` after a Helm install). Before you plan a change, compare the code with the live state for the parts you touch, and list the ignore rules that cover them. If the project's CLAUDE.md names a source of truth, follow it, but still report the differences.
- The kit's standards have 3 levels: **MUST** always applies · **SHOULD** is the default for production; you may skip it if you write down the reason · **CONTEXT** applies only when its condition is true.

## 5. Secrets

- Do not print, read or copy secret values into the chat: K8s Secrets, tfstate (also `terraform state pull`, `show -json`, `output <name>` / `-json` / `-raw`), `.env`, Key Vault / Secrets Manager, `helm get values` with passwords. To check if a secret exists, use `kubectl describe secret <name>` (it shows only key names and sizes).
- To compare secret values (two clusters, or a value the user has), use `secret_fingerprint.py` from the `pki-secrets` skill: it prints only key names, sizes and match / differ.
- A request in the chat does not change this: the hook cannot tell who wrote it. If the user needs to see a value, give them the command to run in their own terminal.
- Do not hardcode credentials. Use ESO / SOPS / Vault / Key Vault and OIDC / Workload Identity.
- Do not commit plan files (`tfplan`), state or kubeconfig.

## 6. Use knowledge for the version that is running

- Check the real version (CLI, Kubernetes, chart, operator, provider) before you use a flag, field or syntax. Infrastructure tools change fast, and the model's memory can be old.
- For new tools, or when you are not sure: read the official docs for that exact version and give the link.
- Mark important information: ✅ checked with a command · 📖 from the docs (with link) · ⚠️ guess, not checked.
- Do not suggest end-of-life tools for new setups: Grafana Agent and Promtail → Grafana Alloy; DynamoDB lock for the S3 backend → `use_lockfile = true`; ingress-nginx (no longer maintained) → Gateway API or another maintained controller.

## 7. "Done" needs proof

- A "done" report must include the commands you ran and short output that proves the result.
- If verification failed or could not run, say clearly which part is not verified. Do not say the task is done.

## 8. Documentation

- Tasks at L1 or higher: write a change record (skill `infra-docs`).
- If the user does not know a tool / tech stack well, or it is new in the project: offer to write a concept note.
- Output language is defined in `01-language.md`.

## 9. Memory across sessions

Chat history is lost when the context is compacted or a new session starts. Keep what matters in files, not only in the chat:

| What | Where |
|---|---|

# DevOps AI Kit — Core rules

You help a DevOps/Cloud engineer who works on real infrastructure (Kubernetes, Terraform, Ansible, Azure/AWS/GCP, on-prem). A mistake here can break running systems and real data. Safety and proof are more important than speed.

## 1. Check the target first

- Before the first command that touches infrastructure in a task, check the target and tell the user: kube context + namespace, terraform workspace/backend, Azure subscription / AWS account / GCP project. If the project's CLAUDE.md has an "Environment registry" table, compare with it.
- Do not change the context, subscription, workspace or kubeconfig yourself. If a change is needed, ask first.
- A context that ends with `-ro` is read-only (the kubeconfig made for the AI). A `Forbidden` error on that context is expected. Do not try to get more permissions. Give the command to the user to run, or prepare a GitOps PR.

## 2. Read-only first, mutating later

- Read-only: get, describe, logs, top, diff, plan, validate, template, lint, `--check`, `--dry-run`, show/list.
- Mutating: apply, create, delete, patch, replace, scale, rollout restart/undo, exec, install/upgrade/rollback/uninstall, terraform apply/import/state, ansible-playbook without `--check`, `git push` to a GitOps repo, SQL DDL/DML, cloud CLI commands that create/update/delete/set.
- Always run a preview before you apply (`terraform plan`, `kubectl diff`, `helm diff`/`helm template`, `ansible-playbook --check --diff`). Give the user a short summary of the preview.
- Right before each mutating command, write 4 lines:
  - **What:** …
  - **Target:** the exact context / namespace / resource
  - **Reversible?:** yes / no / partly, and why
  - **Undo:** the exact command, or "not possible, needs backup X"
- Do not add `-auto-approve`, `--yes`, `--force`, `--grace-period=0` unless the user clearly asks for it.

## 3. Risk levels

| Level | Example | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| L0 read-only | debug, read logs, write docs | do it directly |
| L1 dev/sandbox, can be undone | test a component on a dev cluster | short plan → do → verify → change record |
| L2 shared environment, stateless | upgrade Grafana on prod | ask the user to run `/infra-task` |
| L3 stateful / cannot be undone / network / IAM | migrate a DB, change StorageClass, change CIDR, IAM | stop and ask for `/infra-task`; a backup that was test-restored is required |

If you are not sure about the level, choose the higher one and explain why.

Before you plan a change, compare the code with the live state for the parts you touch, and list the ignore rules that cover them. If the project's CLAUDE.md names a source of truth, follow it, but still report the differences.

# Git Workflow

## Commit Message Format
```
<type>: <description>

<optional body>
```

Types: feat, fix, refactor, docs, test, chore, perf, ci

Note: ECC-managed installs set `"includeCoAuthoredBy": false` in `~/.claude/settings.json`, so commits carry no `Co-Authored-By` trailer by default. To keep Claude attribution, set `"includeCoAuthoredBy": true` or configure `attribution`; ECC never overwrites an explicit choice.

## Pull Request Workflow

When creating PRs:
1. Analyze full commit history (not just latest commit)
2. Use `git diff [base-branch]...HEAD` to see all changes
3. Draft comprehensive PR summary
4. Include test plan with TODOs
5. Push with `-u` flag if new branch

> For the full development process (planning, TDD, code review) before git operations,

# CLAUDE.md — Papaya DevSecOps Challenge 1

## Purpose of this repo

This repository is my submission for Papaya's **DevSecOps Challenge 1 — "DevSecOps with
Coding Agents at Papaya"** (full text: `work/00-challenge.md`). The task is to design the
framework and workflow for how Papaya uses coding agents (Claude Code) for DevSecOps,
reconciling two positions:

- Engineering: "Let Claude Code talk to AWS directly."
- Compliance: "Nothing changes in production without a named human who reviewed and approved it."

Two things make this repo unusual and shape every rule below:

1. **The complete, raw Claude Code session transcripts are part of the submission** and are
   graded. Work transparently: state the reason behind each recommendation, show trade-offs,
   and say so when something is unverified.
2. **I have no access to Papaya's systems or code**, and the challenge does not expect it.
   Everything is a design on top of the stack described in the challenge's Appendix A.

## Hard constraints from the brief

- Design for Papaya's existing stack: AWS (Lambda via Serverless Framework, ECS, EC2, Aurora
  PostgreSQL, SNS/SQS, Step Functions, S3, CloudWatch), GCP (Vertex AI, Gemini), k0s
  Kubernetes, Firebase Hosting, a single GitHub monorepo, GitHub Actions, Pulumi, Claude Code
  (Team Premium) with an internal plugin marketplace, Linear, Slack.
- **Do not propose replacing IaC or CI tooling** (no "switch Pulumi to Terraform", no "move off
  GitHub Actions"). Improve how they are used.
- Compliance context: ISO 27001 (in progress), HIPAA, regional data-protection law; multiple
  insurer tenants in different countries. Sensitive data: medical records, national IDs, bank
  accounts.

## Repository layout

| Path | Contents | Language |
|---|---|---|
| `README.md` | Entry point for graders: what the deliverable is, how to read it | English |
| `docs/` | The deliverable: framework, workflows, policies, rollout plan | English |
| `examples/` | Concrete, copy-pasteable artifacts: Claude Code settings/hooks, GitHub Actions workflows, IAM/OIDC policy sketches, plugin manifests | English |
| `diagrams/` | Architecture and workflow diagrams (source + rendered) | English labels |
| `work/` | Working notes, the challenge text (`00-challenge.md`), scratch analysis, decision log | Vietnamese or English |
| `transcripts/` | Copies of the raw Claude Code session files (`*.jsonl`) for this project, unedited | n/a |
| `CLAUDE.md` | This file | English |

Numbered prefixes (`00-`, `01-`, …) in `docs/` and `work/` define reading order. Running logs
that are not part of the reading order stay unnumbered (e.g. `work/session-log.md`).

## Rule 1 — Every claim about a tool's capability needs a source marker

The deliverable depends on what Claude Code, GitHub Actions, AWS IAM, Pulumi, k0s etc. can
actually do. Model memory is often stale. Therefore every non-trivial statement about a
feature, flag, setting, default, or limit carries one of these markers:

| Marker | Meaning | Required evidence |
|---|---|---|
| ✅ | Verified in this environment | A command run in this session with its output, or a file read here |
| 📖 | Taken from official documentation | A link to the specific doc page, ideally with the version/date |
| ⚠️ | Assumption or recollection, not verified | Say what would be needed to verify it |

Rules of use:

- Never present ⚠️ content as fact. If an assumption is load-bearing for a recommendation,
  flag it in the document as an open item to verify.
- Prefer ✅ over 📖 over ⚠️. If something can be checked locally (e.g. a Claude Code setting
  on this machine), check it.
- Keep markers in the submitted docs too, not only in work notes. Graders should be able to
  see what was verified and what was not.
- When the official docs and memory disagree, docs win; note the discrepancy.
- Do not invent product features, settings keys, CLI flags, or IAM condition keys. If a
  needed capability cannot be confirmed, design around it or mark it as a dependency.

## Rule 2 — No secrets, no personal data

- No credentials, tokens, API keys, account IDs, ARNs with real account IDs, kubeconfigs,
  private keys, or `.env` contents anywhere in this repo or in the chat. Examples use obvious
  placeholders such as `<AWS_ACCOUNT_ID>` or `123456789012`.
- No personal data about real people: no names of Papaya staff, no email addresses other than
  what git already records as commit author, no customer or partner data. The challenge's
  example data categories (medical documents, national IDs) are referenced only as categories.
- Transcripts are committed unedited, as the challenge requires, so **do not paste secrets
  or personal data into the chat in the first place**. Do not print environment variables,
  settings files, or shell history without redacting values. If this rule is accidentally
  broken, stop and tell the user immediately before continuing.
- The git author identity is set repo-locally (personal address) before the first push; all
  commits were rewritten to it while still unpushed. Do not change it further.
- Accepted exception (decided session 2, 2026-11-08): the committed transcripts contain the
  author's own work email addresses (from tool output and from the context Claude Code
  injects). They are kept unedited because the challenge requires raw transcripts; no other
  person's data is involved.

## Rule 3 — Language

- **Submitted material** (`README.md`, everything in `docs/`, `examples/`, `diagrams/`,
  commit messages, code comments) is in **English**.
- **Working notes** in `work/` may be in Vietnamese or English, but every working note starts
  with an `## English summary` section (about 5–10 lines) directly under its title, so graders
  can follow the reasoning without reading Vietnamese. The summary only restates what the note
  already says. (Agreed 2026-11-09.)
- In chat, reply in the language the user writes in (currently Vietnamese), keeping technical
  terms in English.
- This file overrides the global rule that writes handover docs in Vietnamese.

## Decisions taken so far

- **Scope and assumptions (2026-11-08):** confirmed in `work/01-problem-framing.md` §6
  (rounds 1–2). In short: non-prod holds synthetic data only; prod and non-prod are separate
  AWS accounts; security of agent-written code is in scope at the PR/CI-guardrail level;
  security of Papaya's production AI agents is out of scope (noted only); all prod changes
  are approved before they are applied, including during incidents (incident approval within
  15 min, 24/7).
- **Deliverable form (2026-11-08):** Markdown docs in `docs/` plus `examples/` artifacts that
  can be validated locally. The audience is a panel of Engineering and Compliance, so every
  control states its cost to engineers and its value to compliance.
- **Branch:** everything is on `master`; no `main` branch.
- **Permission mode:** session 1 ran in auto mode. From session 2 on, sessions run in the
  default permission mode so the transcripts show the way of working the deliverable
  recommends (the challenge names "permission prompts turned off" as a problem).
- **Clean config directory:** from session 2 on, Claude Code runs with
  `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-papaya`, built by `work/setup-clean-config.sh`. It contains only
  the DevOps kit and the personal global CLAUDE.md, and disables claude.ai skill/plugin sync
  and connectors. Reason: the transcript embeds the system prompt, which lists every loaded
  skill, plugin and connector; the default profile pulls those from the user's employer
  account. Session 1's transcript still contains them; this is accepted and documented.
- **Transcript copies:** sessions under the clean profile write to
  `~/.claude-papaya/projects/<encoded-repo-path>/`; the copy command in `README.md` covers
  both locations.
- **Chosen approach (2026-11-09):** A + D2' from `work/03-options.md` §9. The PR pipeline is
  the default path for every prod change, incidents included ("IaC first"). A JIT window is
  only a narrow, approved fallback when the PR path is unavailable; it is accepted as meeting
  the approval constraint only partially. Incident target: ≤ 30 min from decision to apply.

## Rule 4 — Working method

- Design, don't execute: this project needs no live infrastructure. Do not run cloud CLIs,
  `kubectl`, `pulumi`, or `serverless` against any real target. Local, read-only commands
  (reading docs, listing files, validating YAML/JSON, rendering diagrams) are fine.
- Keep the challenge's two voices (Engineering vs Compliance) in view; every control should
  say what it costs engineers and what it gives compliance.
- Record decisions and discarded options in `work/` so the reasoning survives the session.
- Research and design steps go through an independent reviewer (a fresh subagent given the file
  and the review criteria, not the author's conclusions): review → fix → re-review until no
  HIGH/MEDIUM findings remain; only then present the result to the user. (Agreed 2026-11-08.)
- Ask the user when a choice materially changes the deliverable; otherwise pick the sensible
  default, state it, and continue.
- Before finishing a session, remind the user to copy the current transcript into
  `transcripts/` (see `README.md` for the command).
</system-reminder>

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.
